units.title: FRIENDS AND FAMILY

overview.intro: This unit is about the people closest to you — who they are, how you resemble them, and how you deal with them. At B2 the challenge is no longer listing family members, but describing relationships with precision: how people behave, why they clash, and what holds them together.
goals: Describe personality and family relationships with natural, specific vocabulary.
Use the gerund confidently after common verbs and after every preposition.
Explain and define ideas using noun clauses after ‘be’.
overview.outcome: By the end you can describe a family member in detail, explain who you take after and why, and use at least three verb + gerund patterns without hesitating.

vocab.def: to have a friendly, easy relationship with someone.
vocab.use: Use ‘with’ before the person: get along WITH your sister. On its own it describes the pair: ‘We get along.’ In British English ‘get on with’ is more common.
examples: I get along with my brother far better now that we live apart.
They’ve never really got along, but they stay polite at family dinners.
vocab.colloc: get along well · get along fine · not get along at all

vocab.def: (of a family or group) bound together by strong, warm ties.
vocab.use: Only used before a noun: a close-knit family / community / team. It is always positive.
examples: We’re a close-knit family — nobody makes a big decision alone.
She grew up in a close-knit neighbourhood where everyone knew her name.
vocab.colloc: a close-knit family · a close-knit community · a close-knit team

vocab.def: to resemble an older relative in looks or in character.
vocab.use: Only for relatives, and only for older ones — you take after a parent, never after a friend. Never separable: ‘take after him’, not ‘take him after’.
examples: He takes after his grandfather — same laugh, same stubbornness.
I take after my mother in looks but after my father in temperament.
vocab.colloc: take after your mother / father · really take after someone

vocab.def: relaxed and not easily worried or annoyed.
vocab.use: A compliment about temperament. Compare ‘laid-back’ (very similar, more informal) and ‘lazy’ (negative, not a synonym).
examples: My dad is so easygoing that nothing ever seems to bother him.
She’s easygoing about most things, but not about punctuality.
vocab.colloc: an easygoing person · fairly easygoing · easygoing about something

vocab.def: to form a close emotional connection with someone.
vocab.use: Often used about a shared experience creating the connection: they bonded OVER football.
examples: The cousins bonded over a shared love of cooking.
New parents need time to bond with the baby.
vocab.colloc: bond with someone · bond over something · a strong bond

vocab.def: competition or jealousy between brothers and sisters.
vocab.use: A slightly formal, almost psychological term — useful in discussions and writing rather than casual chat.
examples: A bit of sibling rivalry is normal; constant fighting isn’t.
Their sibling rivalry faded once they both left home.
vocab.colloc: intense sibling rivalry · a healthy sibling rivalry

vocab.def: to slowly become less close to someone, usually without a quarrel.
vocab.use: Intransitive and usually about friendships over time: “We drifted apart after university.”
examples: We were inseparable at school, but we drifted apart in our twenties.
Old friendships drift apart unless somebody makes an effort.
vocab.colloc: gradually drift apart · drift apart over the years

vocab.def: the family member who is seen as different or disapproved of.
vocab.use: Always “the black sheep of the family”. Mildly humorous rather than cruel.
examples: He’s the black sheep of the family — the only one who didn’t study law.
Every family has its black sheep.
vocab.colloc: the black sheep of the family

vocab.def: to repair a relationship after an argument.
vocab.use: Separable with “things”: “patch things up with your sister”. Informal but very common.
examples: They finally patched things up after two years of silence.
I’d like to patch things up before the wedding.
vocab.colloc: patch things up with · patch up a quarrel

vocab.def: caring for someone in a way that helps them grow.
vocab.use: For people and environments: “a nurturing parent”, “a nurturing atmosphere”. The verb is “to nurture”.
examples: She grew up in a nurturing household.
Good teams have a nurturing culture.
vocab.colloc: a nurturing environment · nurture a talent

vocab.term: to rub someone up the wrong way
vocab.def: to irritate someone, often without meaning to.
vocab.use: About a personality clash rather than a single offence: “He rubs me up the wrong way.” American English drops “up”.
examples: She never says anything rude, but she rubs me up the wrong way.
Something about his tone rubbed everyone up the wrong way.
vocab.colloc: rub someone up the wrong way · rub people the wrong way

vocab.def: to agree with someone, usually about something ongoing.
vocab.use: Most common in the negative: “We don’t see eye to eye on money.” Add “with” before the person and “on” before the subject.
examples: My father and I have never seen eye to eye on politics.
They see eye to eye on almost everything except holidays.
vocab.colloc: don’t see eye to eye · see eye to eye with someone on something

grammar.name: Verbs followed by gerunds
grammar.short: enjoy, avoid, mind, keep + -ing — and after every preposition.
grammar.rule: Some verbs are always followed by the -ing form rather than the infinitive: enjoy, avoid, mind, keep, finish, can’t stand, feel like, suggest, consider. In addition, any verb that follows a preposition takes -ing.
form: Verb + -ing: enjoy spending, avoid arguing, keep interrupting, finish talking.
Adjective + preposition + -ing: good at listening, tired of waiting, interested in learning.
Verb + preposition + -ing: insist on paying, look forward to seeing, apologise for being late.
notes: ‘Feel like’ means ‘want’ and always takes -ing: ‘I feel like going out’, never ‘feel like to go’.
‘Look forward to’ ends in the preposition ‘to’, so it takes -ing: ‘looking forward to meeting you’.
To make a gerund negative, put ‘not’ in front: ‘I enjoy not having plans on Sunday.’
examples: I enjoy spending time with my cousins at the weekend.
She can’t stand arguing over nothing.
They’re good at getting along with everyone.
grammar.watch: After a preposition, English always uses -ing — ‘interested in learning’, never ‘interested in to learn’.
grammar.deep: Verb patterns are lexical rather than logical: the verb, not the meaning, decides what can follow it. A large family of verbs — enjoy, avoid, consider, mind, resent, keep, risk, deny, recommend — takes a gerund, because the gerund names the activity as a thing, and these verbs all take a thing as their object. That is why “I avoid arguing” works and “I avoid to argue” does not. Two refinements matter at B2. First, prepositions always take gerunds, so any verb that arrives with a preposition attached (insist on, object to, look forward to, get used to) inherits the gerund: “She insisted on paying.” Second, a handful of verbs accept both forms with a genuine change of meaning — stop, remember, forget, try, go on, regret — and those pairs are worth memorising as contrasting sentences rather than as rules.

chart.title: Verbs followed by gerunds
rows: enjoy, love, hate, mind, resent, can’t stand
keep, carry on, finish, give up, quit
She kept asking the same question.
insist on, object to, look forward to, succeed in
They insisted on seeing the manager.
I stopped smoking. / I stopped to smoke.

more: I can’t stand being told what to do by someone younger than me.
She keeps bringing up an argument we had years ago.
They’ve given up trying to change his mind.
We’re used to being interrupted at family dinners.
He apologised for not calling on my birthday.
Nobody in my family objects to being teased, as long as it stops there.

fix.wrong: I look forward to meet your parents.
fix.right: I look forward to meeting your parents.
fix.why: “To” in “look forward to” is a preposition, so it takes the gerund.

fix.wrong: She suggested to go together.
fix.right: She suggested going together.
fix.why: “Suggest” takes a gerund or a that-clause, never an infinitive.

fix.wrong: I enjoy to spend time with my cousins.
fix.right: I enjoy spending time with my cousins.
fix.why: “Enjoy” belongs to the gerund-only family.

drill.name: Feed the verb
drill.prompt: Complete each verb with a gerund about your own family, then say the same idea again after a preposition.

dialogue.line: Do you mind living with your parents again?
I don’t mind sharing the house. I mind being asked where I’m going.
So you’ve got used to the questions?
I’ve given up answering them, which isn’t the same thing.

contrast.title: Gerund, infinitive, or both
rows: insist on, object to, look forward to
I remember locking it. / Remember to lock it.

grammar.sound: In “look forward to meeting” the two unstressed syllables run together as /tə ˈmiːtɪŋ/. Stressing “to” is what makes learners then reach for the infinitive.

grammar.name: Noun clauses after ‘be’
grammar.short: The problem is that… / What matters is…
grammar.rule: A whole clause can work as a noun. Placed after the verb ‘be’, it defines or explains the subject: ‘The problem is that we never listen.’
form: Noun + be + that-clause: The truth is that we take after our mother.
What-clause + be + noun/clause: What matters is that we stay close.
The reason… + be + that-clause: The reason I called is that I miss you.
notes: ‘That’ can be dropped in speech: ‘The truth is we take after her.’
When the subject is a ‘what’-clause, the verb is singular: ‘What worries me is the silence.’
Word order inside the clause is statement order — no inversion: ‘The question is where he went’, not ‘where did he go’.
examples: The truth is that we take after our mother.
What matters is that we stay close.
The reason I called is that I miss you.
grammar.watch: Say ‘The reason is THAT…’, not ‘The reason is BECAUSE…’ — that repeats the idea twice.
grammar.deep: A noun clause after “be” lets the sentence announce a whole idea as its complement: “The problem is that nobody told her.” Structurally the clause fills the slot a noun would fill, which is why it can be introduced by “that”, by a wh-word, or by “whether”: the point is why he left, the question is whether we can afford it. English uses this pattern constantly in argument and analysis because it front-loads your framing — “the difficulty is…”, “the truth is…”, “my concern is…” — and then delivers the content. Two mechanics keep it clean. “That” is optional in speech but useful in writing when the clause is long, since it signals where the complement begins. And the clause keeps statement word order even after a wh-word, so it is “the question is where he went”, never “where did he go”.

chart.title: Noun clauses after be
rows: The trouble is (that) we started too late.
The issue is what we tell the client.
The question is whether it’s worth it.
The reason he left is that he felt ignored.
What we need is more time.
The point is why she agreed. (not why did she agree)

more: The trouble is that nobody wants to be the one who calls first.
What holds the family together is Sunday lunch, not affection.
The reason she took offence is that she was already exhausted.
My worry is whether he’ll even reply.
What surprised me was how quickly they forgave each other.
The point is not who started it.

fix.wrong: The problem is because we never talk.
fix.right: The problem is that we never talk.
fix.why: “Be” takes a that-clause; “because” cannot follow it.

fix.wrong: The question is where did he go.
fix.right: The question is where he went.
fix.why: A noun clause keeps statement word order, with no inversion.

fix.wrong: What matters are that we stay close.
fix.right: What matters is that we stay close.
fix.why: A what-clause subject is singular.

drill.name: Frame it first
drill.prompt: Say each idea twice: once as a plain sentence, then reframed with a noun clause after “be”.
items: they still argue about the house

dialogue.line: So why aren’t they speaking?
The trouble is that neither of them will call first.
That’s absurd.
What makes it worse is that they both want to.

contrast.title: Which introducer
rows: The problem is that we started late.
The issue is what we tell her.
The question is whether to go.
The reason he left is that he felt ignored.
She never asked, which is why nobody told her.

grammar.sound: Speakers pause very slightly before the that-clause and stress the noun that frames it: “the PROBlem is … that nobody asked”. That pause is what lets a long clause land.

speaking.text: In pairs, two siblings plan a surprise party for a parent but can’t agree on anything – practise getting along and compromising.
This house believes friends can be closer than family. Argue for or against.
Describe someone in your family you take after – in looks and in personality.

tips: After a preposition, always use the -ing form: ‘good at cooking’, ‘interested in learning’.
‘Enjoy, avoid, mind, finish, keep’ are never followed by ‘to’ – say ‘enjoy reading’, not ‘enjoy to read’.
Common slip: ‘The reason is that…’, not ‘The reason is because…’.

quiz.q: I really enjoy ___ time with my family at weekends.
quiz.explain: After ‘enjoy’ we use the gerund: ‘enjoy spending’.

dynamics.name: Family constellation
dynamics.how: Each student sketches four circles for four relatives, then describes each one to a partner using one gerund verb and one noun clause — “What I like about her is…”, “She keeps…”. The partner draws the same diagram from the description alone and compares.
dynamics.payoff: The diagram forces detail about relationships rather than a list of names.

dynamics.name: Confession chain
dynamics.how: Each student adds one gerund confession about family life (“I avoid answering the phone after nine”). Every speaker must repeat the previous person’s confession before adding their own.
dynamics.payoff: Repetition drills the pattern without a worksheet.

dynamics.name: Reframe the row
dynamics.how: Groups are given five blunt statements about a family argument and must reframe each with a noun clause that sounds diplomatic. Groups then read both versions aloud and vote on which they would actually say.
dynamics.payoff: Shows the structure as a politeness tool, not decoration.

dynamics.name: Agony aunt
dynamics.how: Student A presents a family problem; B replies with three sentences, one starting “The problem is…”, one “What you need is…”, one advising with a gerund (“I’d recommend waiting”).
dynamics.payoff: Puts both target structures in one exchange with a real purpose.

writing.title: The relative I understand least
writing.brief: Write about one relative you find difficult to understand. Describe what they do, how you react to it, and what you think holds the relationship together. Frame at least three of your points with noun clauses after “be”.
criteria: Five gerunds, at least two after prepositions.
Three noun clauses after “be”, using different introducers.
No infinitive after a preposition anywhere in the text.

homework.title: Ten gerunds, five frames
homework.task: Write ten true sentences about your family using ten different gerund-taking verbs or prepositions, marking which is which. Then rewrite five of them as noun clauses after “be”, using a different introducer each time.

test.q: I’m looking forward to ___ your parents.
test.explain: “To” here is a preposition, so the gerund follows.

test.q: She suggested ___ the whole thing.
test.explain: “Suggest” takes a gerund or a that-clause.

test.q: The trouble is ___ nobody apologised.
test.explain: A noun clause after “be” is introduced by “that”.

test.q: The question is ___ we tell her tonight.
test.explain: “Whether” presents the two alternatives.

test.q: What matters ___ that we stay in touch.
test.explain: A what-clause subject always takes a singular verb.

board: Two columns at the top: VERB + -ING (enjoy, avoid, mind, keep, give up) and PREPOSITION + -ING (good at, tired of, look forward to).
Under them, one red box: “look forward to MEET” with MEET crossed out and “meeting” written above it.
Middle band: STOP / REMEMBER / TRY written once each, with the gerund meaning on the left and the infinitive meaning on the right.
Lower half: the frame BE + [ that / what / whether / the reason… is that ] with four empty slots for the class to fill.
Side column: a growing list of the framing nouns the class supplies — problem, issue, question, point, truth, worry.

units.title: MISTAKES AND MYSTERIES
units.theme: Past obligation, speculation and unsolved mysteries

overview.intro: This unit is about the past you cannot change and the past you cannot explain. You will learn to talk about what you had to do, what you should have done, and what might, must or can’t have happened — the language of regret, blame and speculation.
goals: Talk about past obligation and criticise past actions politely.
Speculate about the past with modal verbs and different degrees of certainty.
Describe mysteries, evidence and conclusions with precise vocabulary.
overview.outcome: By the end you can retell an unsolved event and offer three theories about it, each with a different level of certainty.

vocab.def: strange and frightening in a mysterious way.
vocab.use: Describes atmosphere rather than people: an eerie silence, an eerie glow. Stronger and stranger than ‘creepy’, which is more personal.
examples: There was an eerie silence in the house after everyone left.
The fog gave the whole street an eerie feel.
vocab.colloc: an eerie silence · an eerie atmosphere · eerily quiet

vocab.def: to understand or solve something after thinking about it.
vocab.use: Separable: figure out the answer / figure it out. Slightly informal; ‘work out’ is the British equivalent.
examples: It took us hours to figure out how he’d got in.
I still can’t figure it out.
vocab.colloc: figure out what happened · figure it out · finally figure something out

vocab.def: a piece of information that helps solve a mystery.
vocab.use: You give, find or follow a clue. ‘Not have a clue’ is a common idiom meaning ‘have no idea’.
examples: The only clue was a muddy footprint by the door.
Honestly, I haven’t got a clue what happened.
vocab.colloc: a vital clue · find / leave a clue · not have a clue

vocab.def: to decide something too quickly, without all the facts.
vocab.use: Almost always a criticism or a warning: ‘Let’s not jump to conclusions.’
examples: Don’t jump to conclusions — we haven’t heard his side yet.
She jumped to conclusions and accused the wrong person.
vocab.colloc: jump to conclusions · let’s not jump to conclusions

vocab.def: impossible to understand; very confusing.
vocab.use: Describes the thing, not the person: a baffling case. The person is ‘baffled’.
examples: The disappearance of the plane remains baffling.
Police were baffled by the lack of evidence.
vocab.colloc: a baffling mystery · utterly baffling · be baffled by something

vocab.def: the person — or thing — responsible for a crime or problem.
vocab.use: Also used humorously for the cause of a small problem: ‘The culprit was a loose wire.’
examples: The culprit turned out to be a neighbour’s cat.
Investigators are still looking for the culprit.
vocab.colloc: catch the culprit · the real culprit · the likely culprit

vocab.def: looking back with the knowledge you have now.
vocab.use: Usually opens the sentence and pairs naturally with past modals: “In hindsight, I should have asked.”
examples: In hindsight, the warning signs were obvious.
With hindsight, we were far too optimistic.
vocab.colloc: in hindsight · with the benefit of hindsight

vocab.def: to make something clearer, to provide an explanation.
vocab.use: Followed by a noun or a wh-clause: “The email sheds light on why he resigned.”
examples: The new evidence sheds light on the whole case.
Nothing shed any light on the disappearance.
vocab.colloc: shed light on a mystery · shed new light on

vocab.def: suggesting something without proving it.
vocab.use: Almost always with “evidence”. Useful when speculating about the past: “The evidence is circumstantial, so she may not have done it.”
examples: The case rests on circumstantial evidence.
It’s circumstantial at best.
vocab.colloc: circumstantial evidence · purely circumstantial

vocab.def: to fail to notice or consider something.
vocab.use: Transitive. Not the same as “oversee” (to supervise), a common confusion.
examples: We overlooked one crucial detail.
Somebody must have overlooked the deadline.
vocab.colloc: easily overlooked · overlook an error

vocab.def: knowing now what nobody knew then.
vocab.use: A formal alternative to “in hindsight”, useful before “should have”: “With the benefit of hindsight, we should have waited.”
examples: With the benefit of hindsight, the decision looks reckless.
Everything is obvious with the benefit of hindsight.
vocab.colloc: with the benefit of hindsight · hindsight is a wonderful thing

grammar.name: Past modals of obligation
grammar.short: had to / should have / was supposed to.
grammar.rule: Different structures express different relationships to a past duty: whether it happened, whether it was necessary, and whether you regret it.
form: had to + verb = a real past obligation that was fulfilled: We had to leave early.
didn’t have to + verb = no obligation existed (and usually it didn’t happen).
should / ought to have + past participle = criticism or regret about the past.
was / were supposed to + verb = an expectation that was probably not met.
notes: ‘Didn’t have to’ and ‘shouldn’t have’ are very different: ‘You didn’t have to pay’ (it wasn’t necessary) vs ‘You shouldn’t have paid’ (it was a mistake).
‘Must’ has no past form for obligation — use ‘had to’.
‘Was supposed to’ strongly implies the thing did NOT happen: ‘She was supposed to lock the door’ — and she didn’t.
examples: We had to leave before midnight.
You should have told me the truth.
She was supposed to lock the door.
grammar.watch: After ‘should have’ use a past participle, not a past simple: ‘should have gone’, never ‘should have went’.
grammar.deep: Past modals of obligation sort themselves into what did happen and what did not. “Had to” reports a real past necessity that was carried out: “I had to renew my passport.” “Should have” and “ought to have” report an obligation that was not met, which is why they always carry criticism or regret: “You should have told me.” “Didn’t have to” and “didn’t need to” report an absence of obligation, and here English draws a fine distinction — “I didn’t have to pay” means no payment was required, while “I needn’t have paid” means I paid unnecessarily. Notice that “must” has no past of its own for obligation; “had to” takes over. The whole family runs on one template — modal + have + past participle — and the reduced pronunciation (“should’ve”, “must’ve”) is what makes them hard to hear rather than hard to build.

chart.title: Past obligation: what happened and what didn’t
rows: I was supposed to send it.

more: We had to hand in our phones before the exam started.
I didn’t have to pay for the second ticket, luckily.
You needn’t have brought anything — there was plenty of food.
She was supposed to lock up, but she left the keys on the desk.
They ought to have warned us about the road closure.
We shouldn’t have signed anything before reading it.

fix.wrong: I must go to the police station yesterday.
fix.right: I had to go to the police station yesterday.
fix.why: “Must” has no past form for obligation; “had to” replaces it.

fix.wrong: You should have went earlier.
fix.right: You should have gone earlier.
fix.why: After “have” comes the past participle, not the past simple.

fix.wrong: I didn’t need to pay, so I paid nothing extra — I needn’t have paid.
fix.right: I didn’t need to pay, so I paid nothing extra.
fix.why: “Needn’t have paid” means the money was actually spent; the two cannot describe the same event.

drill.name: Did it happen?
drill.prompt: For each prompt, say the sentence and then state whether the action was carried out or not.
items: hand in the form / obligatory, done
bring a gift / brought one unnecessarily
tell the manager / not done, regretted

dialogue.line: Why is the alarm still going?
Someone was supposed to reset it at six.
You should have called maintenance.
I did. I needn’t have — they were already on their way.

grammar.sound: “Should have” reduces to /ˈʃʊdə/ and “must have” to /ˈmʌstə/, so the “have” disappears entirely. Learners who pronounce it fully sound formal; those who write “should of” have heard it correctly and spelt it wrongly.

grammar.name: Modals for degrees of certainty about the past
grammar.short: must have / might have / can’t have.
grammar.rule: To draw a conclusion about the past from present evidence, use a modal + have + past participle. The modal you choose shows how sure you are.
form: must have + p.p. = you are almost certain it happened.
might / may / could have + p.p. = it is possible.
can’t / couldn’t have + p.p. = you are almost certain it did NOT happen.
notes: The negative of ‘must have’ in this meaning is ‘can’t have’, not ‘mustn’t have’.
‘Could have’ has two meanings: possibility (‘He could have missed the bus’) and unrealised ability (‘I could have helped, but nobody asked’).
In speech, ‘have’ reduces to /əv/ — which is why learners write the incorrect ‘must of’.
examples: He must have forgotten his keys.
It can’t have been the cat.
They might have taken the wrong turn.
grammar.watch: Write ‘must have’, never ‘must of’ — they sound identical but only one is English.
grammar.deep: Speculating about the past means taking the certainty scale you use for the present and adding “have + past participle”. At the top, “must have” expresses a confident conclusion drawn from evidence: “The lights are off — they must have gone out.” In the middle, “may have”, “might have” and “could have” leave the question open. At the bottom, “can’t have” and “couldn’t have” reject a possibility outright, and note the asymmetry: the negative of deductive “must” is “can’t”, never “mustn’t”, because prohibition has already claimed that form. One extra piece belongs here: “could have” has a second life describing unrealised possibility (“we could have won”), so context decides whether you are deducing or regretting. Adverbs — surely, presumably, evidently, possibly — do the same work in a different slot and combine well with the modals in written argument.

chart.title: Degrees of certainty about the past
rows: She might not have seen it.
We could have caught the train.

more: The door was unlocked, so somebody must have come back for the files.
She might have misread the date — it’s printed very small.
They can’t have finished already; they only started an hour ago.
He may not have seen your message before he left.
The keys were in her coat, so she couldn’t have dropped them outside.
By now the parcel will have reached the depot.

fix.wrong: He mustn’t have known about the meeting.
fix.right: He can’t have known about the meeting.
fix.why: The negative of deductive “must” is “can’t”; “mustn’t” means prohibition.

fix.wrong: She must forgot her password.
fix.right: She must have forgotten her password.
fix.why: Speculation about the past needs “have + past participle”.

fix.wrong: It could have rained — look how wet the road is.
fix.right: It must have rained — look how wet the road is.
fix.why: Clear evidence calls for the confident modal, not the tentative one.

drill.name: Three levels of certainty
drill.prompt: For each clue, give three explanations: one near-certain, one possible, one you can rule out.
items: his coat is still on the chair
all the lights are on at midnight
her phone goes straight to voicemail
the window is open from the inside

dialogue.line: The office was empty at ten in the morning.
They must have had a meeting off-site.
With the lights on and the door unlocked?
Then somebody may have left in a hurry. They can’t have gone far.

contrast.title: How sure are you
rows: She might not have seen it.

grammar.sound: The modal carries the stress and everything after it flattens: “he MUSTə known”, “she CAN’Tə seen it”. In the negative, the contraction is the only audible clue, so it must be crisp.

speaking.text: Two detectives at a crime scene disagree about what must have happened and what can’t have happened.
This house believes some mysteries are better left unsolved. Agree or disagree.
Tell a partner about a time you jumped to conclusions and got it completely wrong.

tips: ‘must have + past participle’ = near-certain it happened; ‘can’t have’ = certain it didn’t.
‘should have + p.p.’ expresses regret or criticism: ‘I should have studied more.’
Common slip: say ‘must have gone’, not ‘must have went’.

quiz.q: The lights are off – they ___ already gone home.
quiz.explain: ‘Must have + past participle’ expresses near-certainty about the past.

dynamics.name: Crime scene on the desk
dynamics.how: Each group receives five odd objects (a single glove, a torn ticket, a receipt) and must produce three explanations ranked by certainty, then defend the ranking against another group’s cross-examination.
dynamics.payoff: Physical evidence generates deduction modals faster than any prompt sheet.

dynamics.name: Regret auction
dynamics.how: Students write three real “should have” sentences about the past month on slips. Slips are shuffled, read out, and the class guesses the author, then advises what the person should do now.
dynamics.payoff: Anonymity makes the regrets genuine and the structure repeats naturally.

dynamics.name: Needn’t or didn’t need to
dynamics.how: Student A reads a situation; B must decide whether the action happened and produce the right form. Ten items each, then swap and compare scores.
dynamics.payoff: Isolates the one distinction in this unit that even strong students miss.

dynamics.name: Unsolved in four facts
dynamics.how: Groups invent an unsolved incident in exactly four facts, one of which is unconfirmed, and swap with another group who must produce a written solution using at least four different past modals.
dynamics.payoff: Writing the puzzle forces precision about what is and is not known.

writing.title: What I still can’t explain
writing.brief: Describe something that happened to you that has never been explained — a lost object, an odd message, a coincidence. Give the facts first, then three theories at three different levels of certainty, and finish with what you should have done at the time.
criteria: Three different certainty modals about the past, correctly ranked.
Two obligation forms, one fulfilled and one unmet.
No “mustn’t have” used for deduction.

homework.title: Six deductions, four regrets
homework.task: Find six small mysteries in your own week (an unexplained noise, an unanswered message) and write one deduction about each with a different modal. Then write four “should have” or “needn’t have” sentences, marking for each whether the action happened.

test.q: The office door was open, so somebody ___ come back.
test.explain: Evidence plus near-certainty calls for “must have”.

test.q: He ___ known — nobody told him.
test.explain: “Can’t have” is the negative of deductive “must have”.

test.q: I ___ brought food; there was already too much.
test.explain: “Needn’t have” means the action was done and was unnecessary.

test.q: We ___ hand in our phones before the exam.
test.explain: A real, fulfilled past obligation takes “had to”.

test.q: You should have ___ me earlier.
test.explain: After “have” comes the past participle.

units.title: EXPLORING NEW CITIES
units.theme: Describing places, contrast and city vs. small-town life

overview.intro: Describing a place well means adding information without starting a new sentence every time. This unit gives you relative clauses to pack detail into one sentence, the correct order for stacked adjectives, and linkers to admit a drawback while defending your opinion.
goals: Describe cities, neighbourhoods and landmarks with vivid, precise adjectives.
Use defining and non-defining relative clauses accurately, with correct punctuation.
Concede and contrast using despite, although and however.
overview.outcome: By the end you can give a two-minute description of a city you know, using at least three relative clauses and two contrast linkers.

vocab.def: full of energetic and noisy activity.
vocab.use: Positive — it suggests life and energy, not stress. Used before nouns: a bustling market.
examples: The old town is a bustling maze of cafes and stalls.
By eight in the morning the port is already bustling.
vocab.colloc: a bustling market · a bustling city centre · bustling with people

vocab.def: a famous building or place that is easily recognised.
vocab.use: Also used figuratively for an important moment: ‘a landmark decision’.
examples: The cathedral is the city’s best-known landmark.
We used the tower as a landmark to find our way back.
vocab.colloc: a famous landmark · a historic landmark · a landmark building

vocab.def: to fully enjoy and absorb the feeling of a place.
vocab.use: Used with atmosphere, sun, culture. Suggests slow, unhurried enjoyment rather than sightseeing.
examples: We sat in the square for an hour just soaking up the atmosphere.
Skip the museums and soak up the street life instead.
vocab.colloc: soak up the atmosphere · soak up the sun · soak up the culture

vocab.def: away from the places tourists usually visit.
vocab.use: Usually positive, implying authenticity. American English often says ‘off the beaten path’.
examples: The best food is always off the beaten track.
We stayed in a village well off the beaten track.
vocab.colloc: somewhere off the beaten track · well off the beaten track

vocab.def: spreading out over a large, untidy area.
vocab.use: Slightly negative or neutral — it suggests size without planning.
examples: The city is a sprawling mass of low houses and highways.
Sprawling suburbs have swallowed the old farmland.
vocab.colloc: a sprawling city · sprawling suburbs · urban sprawl (noun)

vocab.def: attractively old-fashioned and charming.
vocab.use: Careful: applied to people or ideas it can sound patronising. Safest for buildings and villages.
examples: It’s a quaint little town with cobbled streets.
The hotel was quaint rather than comfortable.
vocab.colloc: a quaint village · quaint cottages · rather quaint

vocab.def: to be full of a particular quality or history.
vocab.use: Usually passive, with abstract nouns: “a city steeped in history”, “steeped in tradition”.
examples: The old quarter is steeped in history.
The festival is steeped in local tradition.
vocab.colloc: steeped in history · steeped in tradition

vocab.def: very close to.
vocab.use: Followed by a place: “a stone’s throw from the beach”. Common in travel writing.
examples: The hotel is a stone’s throw from the cathedral.
We were a stone’s throw from the main square.
vocab.colloc: just a stone’s throw from

vocab.def: full of energy, colour and life.
vocab.use: For places, scenes and cultures: “a vibrant nightlife”, “a vibrant arts scene”. Overused, so alternate with “lively”.
examples: The neighbourhood has a vibrant street-food scene.
It’s a vibrant, chaotic, unforgettable city.
vocab.colloc: a vibrant city · vibrant colours

vocab.def: good enough to justify going out of your way.
vocab.use: “Worth” takes a noun or -ing: “worth a detour”, “worth visiting”. Never an infinitive.
examples: The museum is small but well worth a detour.
That village is worth a detour if you have a car.
vocab.colloc: well worth a detour · worth visiting

vocab.def: to appear suddenly and in numbers.
vocab.use: Typical of urban change: “Cafés have sprung up all along the canal.” Intransitive.
examples: Galleries have sprung up in what used to be a warehouse district.
New towers spring up faster than the transport can cope with.
vocab.colloc: spring up everywhere · spring up overnight

grammar.name: Defining & non-defining relative clauses
grammar.short: Which one needs commas — and which forbids ‘that’.
grammar.rule: A defining relative clause identifies which person or thing you mean and is essential; a non-defining clause adds extra information about something already identified.
form: Defining (no commas): The guide who showed us around was brilliant.
Non-defining (commas, never ‘that’): Bogotá, which sits high in the Andes, is chilly.
Place / time / possession: where, when, whose — the street where I grew up.
notes: In a defining clause you can drop the pronoun when it is the object: ‘the city (that) we visited’. You can never drop it in a non-defining clause.
‘That’ is only possible in defining clauses.
A preposition can move to the end in speech: ‘the district that we stayed in’ (formal: ‘in which we stayed’).
examples: The neighbourhood where I grew up has changed completely.
Bogotá, which sits high in the Andes, is chilly all year.
The guide who showed us around was brilliant.
grammar.watch: If you can remove the clause and still know who or what you mean, it needs commas — and ‘which’, not ‘that’.
grammar.deep: The comma is the whole grammar of relative clauses. A defining clause identifies which one you mean and therefore cannot be removed: “The flight that leaves at six is full” tells you which flight. A non-defining clause adds information about something already identified, sits between commas, and can be deleted without damaging the sentence: “The six o’clock flight, which is always full, leaves from gate 4.” Two consequences follow mechanically. “That” is banned from non-defining clauses, so extra information takes “who” or “which”. And the relative pronoun of a defining clause can be omitted when it is the object (“the flight I booked”) but never when it is the subject. In writing, punctuation therefore changes facts, not rhythm: “my brother who lives abroad” implies several brothers; “my brother, who lives abroad,” implies exactly one.

chart.title: Defining vs non-defining
rows: The man who called is waiting.
Mr Ruiz, who called earlier, is waiting.

more: The square where the market used to be is now a car park.
Lisbon, which sits on seven hills, punishes anyone in the wrong shoes.
The architect who designed the station also built the library.
A city that closes at nine is a difficult place to be young in.
My grandmother, whose flat overlooked the port, refused to move inland.
The years when the factories closed changed the whole district.

fix.wrong: Bogotá, that sits high in the Andes, is chilly.
fix.right: Bogotá, which sits high in the Andes, is chilly.
fix.why: A non-defining clause never uses “that”.

fix.wrong: The guide, who showed us around was brilliant.
fix.right: The guide who showed us around was brilliant.
fix.why: A defining clause takes no commas at all, not even one.

fix.wrong: The neighbourhood where I grew up in has changed.
fix.right: The neighbourhood where I grew up has changed.
fix.why: “Where” already contains the preposition, so “in” is redundant.

drill.name: Commas or no commas
drill.prompt: Join each pair into one sentence, then say whether the clause needs commas and why.
items: I visited Porto. It sits on a river.
The street was too steep. We stayed on it.
My cousin lives in Cali. He never leaves.
That’s the museum. It opened last year.
This is the year. Everything changed then.

dialogue.line: Which part did you like best?
The old quarter, which is completely pedestrianised.
Is that the area where the market is?
That’s the one. The square that everyone photographs is just behind it.

grammar.sound: Commas are audible: a non-defining clause is spoken on a lower pitch with a pause on each side. Run it on without those pauses and listeners hear a defining clause.

grammar.name: Order of modifiers
grammar.short: opinion → size → age → shape → colour → origin → material.
grammar.rule: When several adjectives modify one noun, English uses a fixed order. Native speakers never think about it, but breaking it sounds instantly wrong.
form: opinion → size → age → shape → colour → origin → material → NOUN.
a lovely (opinion) little (size) old (age) stone (material) bridge.
a huge modern glass tower · a charming narrow cobbled street.
notes: Three adjectives before a noun is usually the practical maximum; beyond that, split the sentence.
Adjectives of the same type are joined with ‘and’ or commas: ‘a red and white facade’.
Nouns used as modifiers come last, right before the head noun: ‘an old stone bridge’.
examples: a lovely little old stone bridge
a huge modern glass tower
a charming narrow cobbled street
grammar.watch: Size comes before age: ‘a big old house’, not ‘an old big house’.
grammar.deep: English stacks adjectives in a preferred order, and although breaking it is rarely ungrammatical, it always sounds foreign. The sequence runs from the most subjective to the most inherent: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose — “a lovely little old wooden writing desk”. Two practical points matter more than memorising the list. First, native writers rarely stack more than three, so if you find yourself at four, the sentence probably needs a relative clause instead. Second, commas are used between adjectives of the same type (“a cold, wet morning”) but not between different types (“a big red bus”). Nouns used as modifiers stay closest to the head noun (“a leather office chair”), and numbers come before everything else (“the two big cities”).
more: a beautiful narrow cobbled lane
an enormous new glass concert hall
a charming little nineteenth-century Portuguese tile shop
two ugly grey concrete towers
a quiet old residential district
a striking circular wooden pavilion

fix.wrong: an old big house
fix.right: a big old house
fix.why: Size comes before age.

fix.wrong: a Portuguese lovely little café
fix.right: a lovely little Portuguese café
fix.why: Opinion first, origin last.

fix.wrong: a stone charming bridge
fix.right: a charming stone bridge
fix.why: Material sits closest to the noun.

drill.name: Stack three, stack four
drill.prompt: Describe each thing with three adjectives in the correct order, then add a fourth without breaking it.

dialogue.line: How would you describe the hotel?
A lovely little old family place near the port.
And the new one?
A huge grey concrete block. Very efficient, very ugly.

grammar.sound: A long adjective string is spoken as one unstressed run with the main stress on the noun: “a lovely little old stone BRIDGE”. Stressing each adjective sounds like a list, not a description.

grammar.name: Connecting contrasting ideas
grammar.short: despite / although / however — what follows each one.
grammar.rule: All three express contrast, but they are followed by different structures, and that is where mistakes happen.
form: despite / in spite of + noun or -ing: Despite the traffic, we loved it.
although / even though / though + subject + verb: Although it rained, we explored.
however / on the other hand + full sentence, after a semicolon or full stop.
notes: To use ‘despite’ with a clause, add ‘the fact that’: ‘despite the fact that it rained’.
‘However’ is not a conjunction — it cannot join two clauses with only a comma.
‘Even though’ is stronger than ‘although’; ‘though’ can also come at the end in speech: ‘It was expensive, though.’
examples: Despite the traffic, we loved every minute.
Although it rained all weekend, we explored the old town.
It’s expensive; however, it’s worth every peso.
grammar.watch: Never write ‘despite it rained’ — ‘despite’ takes a noun or -ing, never a clause.
grammar.deep: Contrast connectors differ in grammar far more than in meaning, and choosing wrongly is the commonest punctuation error in B2 writing. “Although”, “though”, “even though” and “while” are subordinating conjunctions: they join two clauses inside one sentence. “However”, “nevertheless” and “on the other hand” are adverbs: they connect two separate sentences and take a comma. “Despite” and “in spite of” are prepositions: they must be followed by a noun or a gerund, which is why “despite it was raining” is wrong and “despite the rain” or “despite the fact that it was raining” are right. Get the category right and the punctuation follows automatically; get it wrong and the sentence either runs on or fragments.

chart.title: Connecting and contrasting ideas
rows: Lima is grey, whereas Cusco is bright.
It’s cheap. On the other hand, it’s far.

more: Despite the traffic, we walked everywhere.
In spite of being cheaper, the suburbs feel further away than they are.
Although the city looks chaotic, it runs on time.
Even though rents have doubled, nobody seems to leave.
The nightlife is exhausting; the mornings, however, are silent.
Prices are high. On the other hand, you never need a car.

fix.wrong: Despite it rained, we explored.
fix.right: Despite the rain, we explored.
fix.why: “Despite” takes a noun or a gerund, never a clause.

fix.wrong: Although the traffic, we arrived early.
fix.right: Although the traffic was bad, we arrived early.
fix.why: “Although” needs a subject and a verb.

fix.wrong: However it rained, we explored.
fix.right: It rained. However, we explored.
fix.why: “However” links two sentences and takes a comma; it does not introduce a clause.

drill.name: Same contrast, three ways
drill.prompt: Express each contrast three times: with despite, with although, and with however.
items: far from the centre / well connected

dialogue.line: Would you live there?
Despite the rent, yes.
Even though you’d be an hour from work?
The commute is long. The evenings, however, make up for it.

contrast.title: What follows each connector
rows: Despite the fact that it rained…
… On the other hand, it’s cheap.

grammar.sound: “However” takes a clear pause after it, which is what the comma represents. Said without the pause it collides with the following clause and sounds like “in whatever way”.

speaking.text: A tour guide shows a visitor around your city, pointing out landmarks and hidden spots off the beaten track.
This house believes city life is better than small-town life. Argue for or against.
Describe a place you love using at least two relative clauses and one contrast linker.

tips: Non-defining clauses need commas and never use ‘that’ – use ‘which’ or ‘who’.
‘Despite’ and ‘in spite of’ take a noun or -ing, not a clause: ‘despite the rain’, not ‘despite it rained’.
Common slip: keep adjective order natural – ‘a big old house’, not ‘an old big house’.

quiz.q: Medellín, ___ is known as the City of Eternal Spring, has a mild climate.
quiz.explain: Non-defining clauses (set off by commas) use ‘which’, never ‘that’.

dynamics.name: Two cities, one paragraph
dynamics.how: Each pair takes two cities they both know and writes a six-sentence comparison in which every sentence uses a different contrast connector from the table. They then read it aloud and the class names the connectors they heard.
dynamics.payoff: The table becomes a checklist, so the rarer connectors get used.

dynamics.name: Guess the district
dynamics.how: Each student describes a real neighbourhood in three sentences containing one relative clause and one three-adjective string, without naming it. The group guesses and then challenges any adjective in the wrong order.
dynamics.payoff: Peer correction on modifier order is faster and more memorable than teacher correction.

dynamics.name: Comma referee
dynamics.how: The teacher reads sentences aloud twice, once with non-defining intonation and once without. Students hold up a card marked COMMAS or NO COMMAS and must explain the difference in meaning.
dynamics.payoff: Trains the ear, which is where the punctuation rule actually lives.

dynamics.name: Tourist board pitch
dynamics.how: Groups have five minutes to pitch a small unglamorous town, admitting one drawback with “despite” or “however”. The audience votes for the most honest pitch rather than the most enthusiastic.
dynamics.payoff: Rewards concession, which is the real function of contrast connectors.

writing.title: The city I would live in and the one I couldn’t
writing.brief: Compare two places you know well. Describe each with adjective strings and relative clauses, then explain in the final paragraph why you would live in one and not the other, conceding at least two drawbacks.
criteria: Two defining and two non-defining relative clauses, punctuated correctly.
Three adjective strings of at least three adjectives in the standard order.
Three different contrast connectors, each followed by the right structure.

homework.title: Five clauses, five strings, five contrasts
homework.task: Write five sentences about your own city with relative clauses, marking each as defining or non-defining. Add five noun phrases with three or more adjectives, and five contrast sentences using despite, although and however at least once each.

test.q: Medellín, ___ is known for its climate, has changed enormously.
test.explain: Non-defining clauses use “which”, never “that”.

test.q: That’s the square ___ the market used to be.
test.explain: “Where” refers to a place and already includes the preposition.

test.q: Choose the correct order.
options: a lovely little old stone bridge
a stone lovely old little bridge
an old lovely stone little bridge
test.explain: Opinion → size → age → material → noun.

test.q: ___ the traffic, we walked everywhere.
test.explain: “Despite” is followed by a noun.

test.q: It rained all week. ___, we explored every day.
test.explain: “However” joins two sentences and takes a comma.

Beside it, a red box: “Bogotá, that sits…” with THAT crossed out.

units.title: EARLY BIRDS AND NIGHT OWLS
units.theme: Sleep, daily routines and time-of-day preferences

overview.intro: Routines produce long, repetitive sentences — ‘When I get up, I make coffee, and after I make coffee, I check my phone.’ This unit teaches you to compress them into shorter, more fluent English, and to state the reasons and conditions behind your habits.
goals: Talk about sleep, energy and daily routines with natural expressions.
Shorten time clauses to participle phrases when the subject is shared.
Give reasons and set conditions with because, since, unless and as long as.
overview.outcome: By the end you can describe your ideal day using at least three reduced time clauses and explain two conditions for your best sleep.

vocab.def: to feel most energetic and alert early in the day.
vocab.use: The opposite is ‘a night owl’. Very common in the negative: ‘I’m not a morning person.’
examples: I’m not a morning person — don’t call me before ten.
She’s such a morning person that she runs at five a.m.
vocab.colloc: a real morning person · not a morning person · an early bird

vocab.def: to go to bed.
vocab.use: Casual and friendly — fine with friends, out of place in writing. ‘Hit the hay’ is the same idea.
examples: I’m exhausted; I’m going to hit the sack.
We hit the sack early and were up at dawn.
vocab.colloc: hit the sack early · time to hit the sack

vocab.def: to sleep later than usual in the morning, by choice.
vocab.use: Different from ‘oversleep’, which is accidental and usually a problem.
examples: On Sundays I sleep in until eleven.
I overslept and missed the bus — that’s not the same as sleeping in.
vocab.colloc: sleep in late · get to sleep in · sleep in on weekends

vocab.def: dazed and sluggish after waking or too little sleep.
vocab.use: Temporary state, usually right after waking or after medicine. Not a personality trait.
examples: I felt groggy for the first hour after the alarm.
Too much sleep can leave you just as groggy as too little.
vocab.colloc: feel groggy · wake up groggy · a bit groggy

vocab.def: to relax and calm down, especially at the end of the day.
vocab.use: Note the pronunciation: ‘wind’ rhymes with ‘mind’. The opposite is ‘wind up’ (make someone tense).
examples: I need an hour to wind down before I can sleep.
A hot shower helps me wind down after work.
vocab.colloc: wind down after work · a wind-down routine · help you wind down

vocab.def: getting a lot done; achieving good results.
vocab.use: Describes people, days, meetings and habits. The noun is ‘productivity’.
examples: My most productive hours are between six and nine in the morning.
It was a productive meeting for once.
vocab.colloc: a productive day · highly productive · productive hours

vocab.term: to be a creature of habit
vocab.def: to like doing the same things at the same times.
vocab.use: Describes a person, usually affectionately: “I’m a creature of habit — same café every morning.”
examples: He’s a creature of habit and hates changes to his routine.
We’re all creatures of habit at heart.
vocab.colloc: a real creature of habit

vocab.def: to work or study late into the night.
vocab.use: Intransitive, no object: “She’s been burning the midnight oil all week.”
examples: I burned the midnight oil to finish the proposal.
There’s no need to burn the midnight oil over this.
vocab.colloc: burn the midnight oil

vocab.def: slow and lacking energy.
vocab.use: For people, mornings, markets and machines: “a sluggish start”, “sluggish sales”.
examples: I feel sluggish if I skip breakfast.
The whole team was sluggish after lunch.
vocab.colloc: feel sluggish · a sluggish start

vocab.def: to keep working despite tiredness or difficulty.
vocab.use: With an object or alone: “power through the last chapter”, “I just powered through”.
examples: I powered through the report and sent it at two a.m.
Sometimes you just have to power through.
vocab.colloc: power through the day · power through it

vocab.def: to be completely exhausted.
vocab.use: British and very common in speech: “I was shattered by nine.” Not used before a noun.
examples: After two night shifts I was absolutely shattered.
She looked shattered but insisted on finishing.
vocab.colloc: absolutely shattered · shattered by the end of the day

grammar.name: Reduced time clauses
grammar.short: While I was cooking → While cooking.
grammar.rule: When the time clause and the main clause share the same subject, you can delete the subject and use the -ing form of the verb after before, after, when, while or since.
form: Before going to bed, I read for a while.
After finishing work, she goes for a run.
While waiting for the bus, he answered his emails.
notes: The reduction is only possible when both subjects are identical. ‘While I was cooking, my brother called’ cannot be reduced.
With ‘after’ you may also use the perfect form for a clear sequence: ‘After having finished, she left.’
A reduced clause at the start of a sentence is followed by a comma.
examples: Before going to bed, I always switch off my phone.
After finishing work, she goes straight to the gym.
When feeling tired, take a short break rather than more coffee.
grammar.watch: Never reduce when the subjects differ — ‘While cooking, the phone rang’ says the phone was cooking.
grammar.deep: A reduced time clause deletes the subject and the auxiliary and leaves a participle: “After I had finished the report, I went home” becomes “Having finished the report, I went home.” The reduction is only legal when both clauses share the same subject, because the participle takes its subject from the main clause — which is why “While walking to work, the rain started” is a dangling modifier: grammatically the rain was walking. Three forms cover almost everything: “while / when + -ing” for simultaneous action, “after / before + -ing” for sequence, and “having + participle” when you want to stress that the first action was complete. Reduced clauses are a hallmark of formal written English, so they raise the register of a paragraph immediately — but they also compress meaning, so use them where the relationship between the events is obvious.

chart.title: Reducing time clauses
rows: While I was waiting, I read.
When she saw the bill, she laughed.
On seeing the bill, she laughed.
Because I had finished, I left.
She left after finishing. ✔ / The rain started while walking. ✘

more: Before leaving the house, I check the alarm twice.
After finishing the last email, she shuts the laptop in a drawer.
While waiting for the coffee to brew, I read one article.
Since moving to an earlier shift, I’ve stopped watching television.
When woken suddenly, most people need ten minutes to make sense.
Having eaten too late, I slept badly.

fix.wrong: While cooking, the phone rang.
fix.right: While I was cooking, the phone rang.
fix.why: The subjects differ, so the clause cannot be reduced — as written, the phone was cooking.

fix.wrong: After to finish work, she goes to the gym.
fix.right: After finishing work, she goes to the gym.
fix.why: A reduced time clause uses the -ing form, not the infinitive.

fix.wrong: Before going to bed, my phone is switched off.
fix.right: Before going to bed, I switch my phone off.
fix.why: The reduced clause must share the subject of the main clause, and a passive breaks that link.

drill.name: Cut the subject
drill.prompt: Reduce each clause if the subjects match; if they don’t, say “can’t reduce” and explain.
items: While I was waiting, I answered emails.
After she left, the meeting improved.
Before I go to bed, I read.
When the alarm went off, I ignored it.
Since I moved here, I sleep better.

dialogue.line: How do you manage a five o’clock start?
Before going to bed I put the alarm across the room.
Does that actually work?
After standing up to switch it off, going back to bed feels ridiculous.

contrast.title: Reduce or keep the subject
rows: While I was cooking, I burnt it.
While I was cooking, the phone rang.
When he was asked, he agreed.
Since I moved, I sleep better.

grammar.sound: The reduced clause is spoken as one unstressed run ending in a slight rise: “before going to BED ↑ … I switch my phone off”. That rise is what tells listeners the sentence has not finished.

grammar.name: Clauses of reason and condition
grammar.short: because / since / as — if / unless / as long as.
grammar.rule: Reason clauses explain why; condition clauses state what must be true for the result to happen. Both attach to the main clause with a subordinating conjunction.
form: Reason: because / since / as + subject + verb.
Condition: if / unless / as long as / provided that + subject + verb.
Either clause can come first; put a comma after it when it does.
notes: ‘Since’ and ‘as’ introduce a reason the listener already knows; ‘because’ gives new, important information.
‘Unless’ = ‘if… not’, so it is already negative.
In condition clauses about the future, use the present tense: ‘As long as it stays quiet, I’ll finish tonight.’
examples: Since I’m an early bird, I schedule my meetings in the morning.
Unless I sleep eight hours, I’m groggy all day.
As long as it’s quiet, I can focus anywhere.
grammar.watch: Don’t add a second negative after ‘unless’: ‘unless I sleep’, not ‘unless I don’t sleep’.
grammar.deep: Reason and condition clauses are the connective tissue of argument, and B2 writing is judged largely on the precision of these choices. For reason, “because” carries new information and usually follows the main clause, while “since” and “as” present the reason as already known and usually come first. For condition, English offers a graded set: “if” is neutral, “unless” means if not, “provided that” and “as long as” impose a requirement, “in case” describes a precaution taken in advance, and “whether or not” cancels the condition entirely. Two traps recur. “Unless” is inherently negative, so the verb after it stays positive. And “in case” is not a synonym of “if”: you take an umbrella in case it rains — before knowing — but you open it if it rains.

chart.title: Clauses of reason and condition
rows: We stopped because the road was closed.
If it rains, we’ll move inside.
Unless you book, you won’t get in.
You can stay as long as you help.
Take cash in case the card fails.
We’re going whether or not it rains.

more: Since the trains start at five, I can be at work before anyone else.
As I sleep badly in the heat, summer nights are a write-off.
Unless I get seven hours, I’m useless by three in the afternoon.
As long as I keep the same bedtime, the early start is fine.
Provided that nobody calls before nine, mornings are the best part of my day.
I don’t set an alarm at weekends, because the light wakes me anyway.

fix.wrong: Unless I don’t sleep well, I’m tired.
fix.right: Unless I sleep well, I’m tired.
fix.why: “Unless” already means “if not”, so a second negative reverses the meaning.

fix.wrong: Because of I was tired, I left early.
fix.right: Because I was tired, I left early.
fix.why: “Because of” takes a noun; “because” takes a clause.

fix.wrong: As long as I will finish by six, I’m happy.
fix.right: As long as I finish by six, I’m happy.
fix.why: Condition clauses use the present, not “will”.

drill.name: Reason, then condition
drill.prompt: Give each fact a reason clause, then restate it as a condition.
items: I go to bed at ten

dialogue.line: Could you start at seven?
As long as I can finish at three, yes.
And if we need you later?
Unless it’s urgent, I’d rather not. Since I get up at five, evenings are gone.

contrast.title: Reason and condition
rows: As long as I finish by six…
I set two alarms in case one fails.

grammar.sound: When the subordinate clause comes first, the comma is a real pause and the clause ends on a rise; when it comes second, there is no pause at all. Moving the clause changes the melody, not the grammar.

speaking.text: A sleep coach advises a client who can’t fall asleep – give and respond to routine advice.
This house believes the world is designed for morning people. Agree or disagree.
Compare your ideal daily routine with a partner’s – who is the real early bird?

tips: You can only reduce a time clause when both clauses have the same subject.
‘Unless’ already means ‘if… not’ – don’t add a second negative after it.
Common slip: ‘before / after + -ing’, not ‘+ to’: ‘after eating’, not ‘after to eat’.

quiz.q: ___ going to bed, I always switch off my phone.
quiz.explain: A reduced time clause uses before / after / while + -ing: ‘Before going to bed’.

dynamics.name: Routine swap
dynamics.how: Partners exchange written morning routines, then retell the other person’s day out loud using only reduced clauses — “After switching off two alarms, he…”. The owner corrects any reduction where the subject changed.
dynamics.payoff: The correction step targets the dangling-participle error precisely.

dynamics.name: Owl versus lark debate
dynamics.how: Teams argue for early or late schedules. Every claim must be supported by a reason clause and every concession by a condition clause; the referee tallies both and stops any bare assertion.
dynamics.payoff: Forces both clause types into genuinely persuasive use.

dynamics.name: Unless trap
dynamics.how: The teacher reads “if not” sentences at speed; students must convert them to “unless” without adding a negative. Any double negative loses the turn.
dynamics.payoff: Isolates the single most persistent error with unless.

dynamics.name: Shift-work rota
dynamics.how: Groups must staff a 24-hour café with four people whose sleep patterns are given on cards, and justify every placement with a reason or condition clause. Rotas that leave a gap must be renegotiated aloud.
dynamics.payoff: A real constraint means the structures are used to solve something.

writing.title: My worst hour of the day
writing.brief: Describe the hour of the day when you function least well, and how your routine is built around it. Use reduced time clauses for the sequence and reason and condition clauses to explain the arrangements you have made.
criteria: Four reduced time clauses, all sharing the subject of the main clause.
Two reason clauses and two condition clauses, using different connectors.
One “unless” sentence with no double negative.

homework.title: Reduce ten, condition five
homework.task: Write ten sentences about your daily routine with full time clauses, then rewrite each in reduced form, marking any that cannot be reduced and why. Add five conditions about your ideal schedule using if, unless and as long as.

test.q: ___ going to bed, I switch off my phone.
test.explain: A reduced time clause takes before / after / while / when + -ing.

test.q: Which sentence is correct?
options: While to wait, I answered emails.
test.explain: The reduced clause must share the subject of the main clause.

test.q: ___ I sleep seven hours, I’m useless by three.
test.explain: “Unless” means “if not” and takes no extra negative.

test.q: ___ the noise, I couldn’t sleep.
test.explain: “Because of” is followed by a noun.

test.q: As long as I ___ by six, I’m happy.
test.explain: Condition clauses use the present tense, not “will”.
