Beside it, a red box: “While cooking, the phone rang” with an arrow to “the phone was cooking?”
Centre band: SAME SUBJECT → reduce / DIFFERENT SUBJECT → keep it, written large.
Lower left: REASON — because / since / as + clause, because of + noun.
Lower right: CONDITION — if / unless / as long as / provided that, with UNLESS = IF NOT and a crossed-out double negative underneath.

units.title: COMMUNICATION
units.theme: Personality types and commenting on communication behaviour

overview.intro: This unit is about how people talk — the blunt, the tactful, the ones who never get to the point — and about how you judge that behaviour out loud. The structure ‘It’s + adjective + to…’ lets you comment on behaviour without attacking a person.
goals: Describe communication styles and personality with accurate adjectives.
Comment on behaviour using ‘It’s + adjective / noun + infinitive’.
Use gerunds as subjects to make general statements.
overview.outcome: By the end you can describe your own communication style and give three pieces of advice using impersonal ‘It’s… to…’ structures.

vocab.def: expressing strong opinions openly, even when others disagree.
vocab.use: Neutral to positive — it suggests courage. ‘Blunt’ and ‘tactless’ are the negative versions.
examples: She’s an outspoken critic of the new policy.
He’s outspoken, but he’s never cruel.
vocab.colloc: an outspoken critic · outspoken about something · remarkably outspoken

vocab.def: to avoid saying something directly.
vocab.use: Nearly always a criticism, often as an instruction: ‘Stop beating around the bush.’
examples: Stop beating around the bush and tell me what happened.
He beat around the bush for ten minutes before mentioning the money.
vocab.colloc: stop beating around the bush · no point beating around the bush

vocab.def: careful not to say things that upset people.
vocab.use: About delivery, not honesty — you can be tactful and truthful at once. The noun is ‘tact’.
examples: That was a tactful way of saying no.
She’s tactful enough to criticise without offending.
vocab.colloc: a tactful reply · be tactful about something · show tact

vocab.def: to give a particular impression to other people.
vocab.use: About perception, not reality — which is why it pairs with ‘although in fact…’.
examples: He comes across as arrogant, although he’s actually shy.
Try to come across as confident in the interview.
vocab.colloc: come across as rude / friendly · come across well

vocab.def: quiet and not showing feelings or opinions easily.
vocab.use: Neutral, unlike ‘cold’ or ‘unfriendly’. Describes temperament, not mood.
examples: He’s reserved at first, but very warm once you know him.
In meetings she stays reserved and listens.
vocab.colloc: quite reserved · a reserved manner · reserved by nature

vocab.term: to get straight to the point
vocab.def: to say the main thing at once, with no extra talk.
vocab.use: Positive in professional contexts; the direct opposite of ‘beat around the bush’.
examples: I’ll get straight to the point: we need the report by Friday.
She always gets straight to the point in meetings.
vocab.colloc: get straight to the point · come to the point

vocab.def: to soften what you say — almost always used in the negative.
vocab.use: “She doesn’t mince her words” means she is direct, even blunt.
examples: He never minces his words in meetings.
She didn’t mince her words about the delay.
vocab.colloc: not mince your words

vocab.def: to misunderstand each other because you are talking about different things.
vocab.use: Usually with “be”: “I think we’re talking at cross purposes.” A polite way to reset a confused conversation.
examples: We were at cross purposes for ten minutes.
I think we’re talking at cross purposes here.
vocab.colloc: be at cross purposes

vocab.def: honest and direct, even about uncomfortable things.
vocab.use: “Candid about + noun”: “candid about her mistakes”. The noun is “candour”.
examples: She was refreshingly candid about the company’s problems.
To be candid, I don’t think it will work.
vocab.colloc: brutally candid · candid about · to be candid

vocab.def: to understand a hidden meaning.
vocab.use: No object: “If you read between the lines, he’s resigning.”
examples: Read between the lines — she isn’t happy about it.
You have to read between the lines with him.
vocab.colloc: read between the lines

vocab.def: to keep speaking while another person is trying to.
vocab.use: Separable: “he talked me over” is wrong — say “he talked over me”. Always critical.
examples: She talks over everyone in meetings without noticing.
It’s hard to make a point when someone talks over you.
vocab.colloc: talk over someone · keep talking over people

vocab.def: to make bad news sound gentler than it is.
vocab.use: Transitive, often in the negative: “I won’t sugar-coat it.”
examples: Don’t sugar-coat the feedback — I’d rather know.
He sugar-coated the numbers and nobody acted on them.
vocab.colloc: sugar-coat the truth · not sugar-coat it

grammar.name: It’s + adjective / noun + infinitive
grammar.short: Comment on behaviour without blaming a person.
grammar.rule: ‘It’ stands in for a later infinitive phrase, letting you evaluate an action in general: ‘It’s rude to interrupt.’ To name the person, add ‘for someone’ or, with adjectives of character, ‘of someone’.
form: It’s + adjective + to + verb: It’s important to listen carefully.
It’s + a / an + noun + to + verb: It’s a mistake to beat around the bush.
It’s + adjective + FOR someone + to + verb: It’s hard for him to say sorry.
It’s + adjective + OF someone + to + verb: It was kind of you to call.
notes: Use ‘of’ when the adjective judges the person (kind, rude, generous); ‘for’ when it judges the difficulty (hard, easy, important).
The same idea can be turned round with a gerund subject: ‘Interrupting people is rude.’
The gerund version sounds more general and more written; the ‘It’s…’ version is more common in speech.
examples: It’s important to listen carefully before replying.
It’s a mistake to beat around the bush at work.
Being tactful takes practice.
grammar.watch: After ‘It’s + adjective’ use the infinitive, not -ing: ‘It’s easy to say sorry’, not ‘It’s easy saying sorry’.
grammar.deep: “It” + adjective or noun + infinitive is English’s way of making a general evaluation without naming a subject: “It’s difficult to say no”, “It’s a mistake to ignore feedback”. The “it” is a placeholder — the real subject is the infinitive clause at the end — and English prefers this order because it delays the heavy information, which keeps sentences readable. Two extensions are worth having. Add “for + person” to specify who: “It’s hard for beginners to hear the difference.” Add “of + person” when the adjective judges character rather than difficulty: “It was kind of you to call.” The distinction is real: “for” describes the situation, “of” describes the person. And “it’s + adjective + that” is the alternative when you want a full clause rather than an infinitive.

chart.title: It + adjective / noun + infinitive
rows: It’s easy for her to say that.
It was rude of him to interrupt.
It’s a shame to waste it.

more: It’s pointless to argue with someone who has already decided.
It’s a relief to hear somebody admit they were wrong.
It’s unrealistic to expect people to say what they mean every time.
It was generous of her to apologise first.
It’s difficult for me to be blunt with people I like.
It’s bad manners to check your phone while someone is explaining something.

fix.wrong: It’s easy saying sorry.
fix.right: It’s easy to say sorry.
fix.why: After “it’s + adjective” English uses the infinitive.

fix.wrong: It’s rude of interrupt.
fix.right: It’s rude to interrupt.
fix.why: The infinitive follows directly; “of” only appears before a person.

fix.wrong: It was kind for her to call.
fix.right: It was kind of her to call.
fix.why: Judging a person’s behaviour takes “of”; “for” marks difficulty or necessity.

drill.name: Judge the behaviour
drill.prompt: Comment on each behaviour twice: once generally, once naming the person with of or for.

dialogue.line: Should I tell him the presentation was weak?
It’s always better to say it early.
It feels harsh.
It would be worse to let him repeat it. And it was decent of him to ask.

contrast.title: of or for, adjective or noun
rows: It was kind of her to call.
It’s hard for me to say no.

grammar.sound: “It’s” is compressed almost to nothing and the stress lands on the adjective: “ts RUDE to interrupt”. Learners who give “it is” full weight sound like they are reading.

grammar.name: Gerunds as subjects
grammar.short: Listening is a skill.
grammar.rule: An -ing form can act as the subject of a sentence, naming an activity in general. It always takes a singular verb.
form: Gerund + singular verb: Listening carefully saves time.
Negative: Not answering messages is rude.
With an object: Interrupting people during meetings annoys everyone.
notes: Never use an infinitive as the subject in everyday English: ‘To listen is a skill’ sounds literary or biblical.
Two gerund subjects joined by ‘and’ take a plural verb: ‘Listening and asking questions help.’
Gerund subjects are common in written arguments and in advice.
examples: Being tactful takes practice.
Interrupting people is the fastest way to lose an argument.
Not saying what you mean creates confusion.
grammar.watch: Keep the verb singular: ‘Listening is important’, not ‘Listening are important’.
grammar.deep: A gerund can serve as the subject of a sentence, and when it does it names an activity as a topic: “Interrupting people is rude.” This is the natural subject form for generalisations, which is why it dominates academic and reflective writing. Three points make it work. The gerund subject is always singular, so it takes a singular verb even when the phrase is long: “Learning two languages at once is demanding.” It can take its own object and modifiers, forming a whole phrase that behaves as one noun. And it competes with the “it + infinitive” pattern you have just met — “Being honest is difficult” and “It’s difficult to be honest” say the same thing, with the gerund version foregrounding the activity and the “it” version foregrounding the judgement. Choosing between them is a matter of emphasis, and alternating keeps a paragraph from sounding mechanical.

chart.title: Gerunds as subjects
rows: Telling him the truth was hard.
It saves time to listen carefully.

more: Listening properly costs nothing and changes everything.
Not answering a difficult message is itself an answer.
Being direct saves time but makes enemies.
Talking over people wins the argument and loses the room.
Admitting you don’t know is the fastest way to be trusted.
Saying “we should catch up” without a date means nothing.

fix.wrong: To listen carefully save time.
fix.right: Listening carefully saves time.
fix.why: A gerund subject is singular, and the gerund is the natural subject form for a general activity.

fix.wrong: Don’t answering messages is rude.
fix.right: Not answering messages is rude.
fix.why: A gerund is negated with “not” immediately before it.

fix.wrong: Interrupting people annoy everyone.
fix.right: Interrupting people annoys everyone.
fix.why: The gerund, not the plural object, controls the verb.

drill.name: Activity as subject
drill.prompt: Turn each behaviour into a gerund subject and finish the sentence with a judgement.

dialogue.line: What annoys you most at work?
Being asked a question by someone who then talks over the answer.
That’s specific.
Not listening is one thing. Pretending to listen is worse.

grammar.sound: A gerund subject takes the main stress and the verb after it stays short: “LISTening carefully SAVES time.” Two stresses, nothing in between.

speaking.text: A manager gives feedback to an employee who is too blunt with clients – stay tactful throughout.
This house believes it’s always better to be direct than polite. Argue for or against.
Describe your communication style – are you outspoken or reserved? Give examples.

tips: After ‘It’s + adjective’, use the infinitive: ‘It’s easy to say sorry.’
When an action is the subject of a sentence, use the -ing form: ‘Listening is a skill.’
Common slip: ‘It’s important to be…’, not ‘It’s important being…’.

quiz.q: It’s not always easy ___ what you really think.
quiz.explain: After ‘It’s + adjective’ we use the infinitive: ‘easy to say’.

dynamics.name: Blunt or tactful
dynamics.how: Each pair receives eight blunt sentences and must produce a tactful version of each using “it’s + adjective + to”. Pairs then read both aloud and the class decides which situations actually needed the blunt version.
dynamics.payoff: The structure becomes a register tool rather than a pattern.

dynamics.name: Communication court
dynamics.how: One student describes a real communication annoyance; the group judges it with “It was rude of…”, “It’s understandable that…” and one gerund-subject verdict. Every judgement must use a different frame.
dynamics.payoff: Judgement language appears naturally when there is something to judge.

dynamics.name: Headline gerunds
dynamics.how: Groups write six workplace-advice headlines, each beginning with a gerund subject, then rank them from most to least useful and defend the top one.
dynamics.payoff: Headlines put the gerund in subject position without any prompting.

dynamics.name: Silent minute
dynamics.how: Two students discuss a topic while the rest listen in silence, then everyone writes three observations using it-clauses or gerund subjects. Observations are read out and the two speakers respond.
dynamics.payoff: Real evidence to comment on makes the structures precise instead of generic.

writing.title: The way we talk to each other at work
writing.brief: Describe the communication habits of a group you belong to — a team, a class, a family. Judge three of those habits with it-clauses and open at least two paragraphs with a gerund subject.
criteria: Four it + infinitive frames, including one with “of” and one with “for”.
Three gerund subjects with singular verbs, one of them negative.
No gerund after “it’s + adjective”.

homework.title: Eight judgements, four subjects
homework.task: Write eight sentences judging communication behaviour with “it’s + adjective or noun + to”, using “of” twice and “for” twice. Then write four sentences whose subject is a gerund, one of them negative.

test.q: It’s not always easy ___ what you really think.
test.explain: “It’s + adjective” takes the infinitive.

test.q: It was very kind ___ her to call.
test.explain: Judging a person’s behaviour uses “of”.

test.q: It’s hard ___ me to be blunt.
test.explain: “For” marks difficulty for a person.

test.q: ___ properly saves everyone time.
test.explain: A gerund can be the subject of a sentence.

test.q: ___ messages is a kind of answer.
test.explain: A gerund is negated with “not” in front of it.

board: Top: IT’S + [adjective / a noun] + TO + verb, written large with two empty slots.
Under it, two branches: OF + person = their behaviour · FOR + person = difficulty for them.
A red box: “It’s easy saying sorry” with SAYING crossed out and “to say” above it.
Lower half: -ING AS SUBJECT with three examples and the verb underlined singular each time.
Side strip: NOT + -ing, with “Don’t answering” crossed out.

units.title: WHAT’S THE REAL STORY?
units.theme: Rumours, journalism and unravelling a story

overview.intro: News language lives on the border between past and present: what has just happened, what happened last night, and what had already happened before that. This unit sorts out those tenses so you can report events clearly and say exactly when they belong.
goals: Talk about news, rumours and reliability with journalistic vocabulary.
Choose correctly between present perfect and simple past.
Order past events with the past perfect and time adverbs.
overview.outcome: By the end you can report a story in three tenses — what had happened before, what happened, and what has happened since.

vocab.def: to be the first to report important news.
vocab.use: Also used intransitively about the news itself: ‘The story broke last night.’
examples: A local paper broke the story before the national media.
The scandal broke just after the election.
vocab.colloc: break a story · the story broke · breaking news

vocab.def: information passed around that may not be true.
vocab.use: Common patterns: ‘there’s a rumour that…’, ‘rumour has it that…’. Spelled ‘rumor’ in American English.
examples: There’s a rumour that the factory is closing.
Rumour has it they’ve already signed the deal.
vocab.colloc: spread a rumour · deny a rumour · rumour has it

vocab.term: to get to the bottom of
vocab.def: to discover the real truth about something.
vocab.use: Followed by a noun or a wh-clause: get to the bottom of it / of what happened.
examples: We need to get to the bottom of this before we accuse anyone.
It took months to get to the bottom of the story.
vocab.colloc: get to the bottom of it · get to the bottom of the matter

vocab.def: unfairly favouring one side; not neutral.
vocab.use: Take the preposition ‘towards’ or ‘against’. The noun is ‘bias’; the neutral opposite is ‘impartial’.
examples: The report was clearly biased against small businesses.
Everyone is biased — good journalism just admits it.
vocab.colloc: biased against / towards · politically biased · media bias

vocab.def: a person who personally saw an event happen.
vocab.use: Stronger than ‘witness’ because it stresses seeing. Common as a modifier: an eyewitness account.
examples: Two eyewitnesses gave completely different versions.
Eyewitness accounts are famously unreliable.
vocab.colloc: an eyewitness account · according to eyewitnesses

vocab.def: to make something seem far more important than it is.
vocab.use: Usually passive: ‘It’s been blown out of proportion.’ A common way to defend someone.
examples: The whole incident was blown out of proportion by the press.
Don’t blow it out of proportion — it was one comment.
vocab.colloc: blown out of all proportion · blow something out of proportion

vocab.term: to take with a pinch of salt
vocab.def: to treat information as possibly exaggerated.
vocab.use: “Take something with a pinch of salt” (UK) or “a grain of salt” (US).
examples: Take those figures with a pinch of salt.
I’d take his version with a large pinch of salt.
vocab.colloc: take it with a pinch of salt

vocab.def: to confirm a claim with independent evidence.
vocab.use: Formal, transitive: “Two witnesses corroborated her account.” Noun: corroboration.
examples: Nothing has corroborated the original story.
We need a second source to corroborate it.
vocab.colloc: corroborate a claim · corroborating evidence

vocab.def: to change your position after saying something else.
vocab.use: Intransitive, often with “on”: “The minister backtracked on the promise.”
examples: The company backtracked within hours.
He backtracked on his earlier statement.
vocab.colloc: backtrack on a promise · quickly backtrack

vocab.def: not supported by evidence.
vocab.use: Almost always before a noun: “unsubstantiated claims”, “unsubstantiated rumours”.
examples: The report contains unsubstantiated allegations.
So far the claims are unsubstantiated.
vocab.colloc: unsubstantiated claims · remain unsubstantiated

grammar.name: Present perfect vs. simple past
grammar.short: Connected to now, or finished and dated.
grammar.rule: Use the present perfect for past actions with a present result or inside unfinished time; use the simple past for finished actions at a definite past time.
form: Present perfect: have / has + past participle — Reporters have uncovered new evidence.
Simple past: The story broke last night.
Unfinished time: this week, today, so far, ever, never → present perfect.
notes: A definite past time expression (yesterday, in 2019, last night) forces the simple past.
In questions, ‘Have you ever…?’ asks about experience; ‘Did you…?’ asks about a known occasion.
American English often prefers the simple past where British English uses the perfect: ‘Did you eat yet?’ vs ‘Have you eaten yet?’
examples: Reporters have uncovered new evidence this week.
The story broke last night.
I’ve never seen a headline like it.
grammar.watch: Never combine the present perfect with a finished time: ‘I have seen him yesterday’ is wrong.
grammar.deep: The choice between these two tenses is not about how long ago something happened but about whether the time frame is closed. The simple past requires a finished period — yesterday, in 2019, last quarter — and reports the event as complete in itself. The present perfect requires an unfinished period (today, this week, in my career) or no time expression at all, and it presents the event as relevant now: “Sales have fallen” invites a discussion about the present situation, while “Sales fell” reads as history. In news writing this produces a reliable pattern: the headline event arrives in the present perfect and the details follow in the simple past. Note also that a defined time can be implied rather than stated, which is why “Did you enjoy it?” as you leave the cinema is more natural than the perfect — the event is visibly over.

chart.title: Present perfect vs simple past
rows: The board approved it last week.
We’ve approved three projects this quarter.
She resigned, packed up and left.
Profits have fallen. They dropped 8% in June.

more: Reporters have found three more documents this week.
The paper published the first version on Tuesday and withdrew it on Wednesday.
I’ve never read a retraction that long.
She left the paper in March; since then nobody has covered the story properly.
Have you seen the correction they printed?
We spoke to the source twice last year, but we haven’t heard from her since.

fix.wrong: I have seen him yesterday.
fix.right: I saw him yesterday.
fix.why: A finished time expression forces the simple past.

fix.wrong: The story broke already.
fix.right: The story has already broken.
fix.why: “Already” with a present result belongs to the present perfect.

fix.wrong: She has left the paper in March.
fix.right: She left the paper in March.
fix.why: A dated event takes the simple past.

drill.name: Dated or not
drill.prompt: Say each fact twice: once with a definite past time and once inside unfinished time, changing the tense accordingly.

dialogue.line: Has the paper responded?
They issued a statement last night.
And since then?
Nothing. They haven’t answered a single question this morning.

grammar.sound: “Have” and “has” reduce to /əv/ and /əz/ and attach to the subject: “they’ve”, “she’s”. The tense is carried by the participle, so the participle must be clear.

grammar.name: Present perfect vs. present perfect continuous
grammar.short: Result and quantity, or activity and duration.
grammar.rule: The simple form focuses on the completed result or how many; the continuous focuses on the activity itself and how long.
form: Simple: has / have + p.p. — She has written three articles.
Continuous: has / have been + -ing — She has been writing since dawn.
Duration: for six months / since March → usually continuous.
notes: State verbs (know, be, believe, own) are not normally used in the continuous.
The continuous can suggest the activity is unfinished, or that its effects are visible: ‘She’s been crying.’
With ‘how long’, both are possible with live/work/study, with almost no difference in meaning.
examples: She has written the report already.
She has been writing since dawn.
They’ve been investigating the case for weeks.
grammar.watch: Use the simple form when you say how many: ‘I’ve read three articles’, not ‘I’ve been reading three articles’.
grammar.deep: Once the perfect is established, the second decision is simple versus continuous, and it turns on what you are counting. The continuous counts time and activity: “I’ve been reviewing contracts all morning” foregrounds the effort and its duration, and often carries a note of complaint or explanation. The simple counts completions and quantities: “I’ve reviewed four contracts” foregrounds the result. Both can be true simultaneously, so the choice is rhetorical rather than factual. Two constraints apply. State verbs — know, own, believe, belong — stay simple, because there is no activity to be in progress. And with live, work and study over a long period, both forms are acceptable with almost no difference in meaning, which is why they make poor practice examples: test yourself on “write”, “read” and “try” instead.

chart.title: Perfect simple vs perfect continuous
rows: I’ve been waiting for two hours.
You’re out of breath — have you been running?

more: She’s written three pieces about it and none of them was printed.
She’s been writing about the case since February.
They’ve interviewed eleven people so far.
They’ve been interviewing witnesses all week.
I’ve read the file twice.
I’ve been reading the file all morning and I’m still on page ten.

fix.wrong: I’ve been reading three articles.
fix.right: I’ve read three articles.
fix.why: A number counts results, which the simple form expresses.

fix.wrong: She has been knowing the source for years.
fix.right: She has known the source for years.
fix.why: State verbs like know do not take the continuous.

fix.wrong: They’ve investigated since March.
fix.right: They’ve been investigating since March.
fix.why: With a duration and an ongoing activity, the continuous is natural.

drill.name: How many or how long
drill.prompt: For each item, produce one sentence with a number and one with a duration, choosing the right form each time.

dialogue.line: How’s the investigation going?
We’ve spoken to nine people.
In how long?
We’ve been working on it since February, and we still haven’t found the original file.

grammar.sound: In the continuous, “been” is unstressed and almost swallowed: “she’z bin RIting”. Dropping it entirely is the commonest audible error at this level.

grammar.name: Past perfect and time adverbs
grammar.short: The earlier of two past events.
grammar.rule: The past perfect (had + past participle) marks the event that happened first when you are already talking about the past. Adverbs like already, just, never and yet sit between the auxiliary and the participle.
form: had + past participle: By the time we arrived, the crowd had already left.
Negative: He had never spoken to the press before.
With adverb: The editor had just finished when the news broke.
notes: If the order of events is obvious from ‘before’ or ‘after’, the past perfect becomes optional.
‘Yet’ goes at the end of negatives and questions; ‘already’ goes in mid-position.
In reported speech, a past simple in the original usually shifts to the past perfect.
examples: By the time we arrived, the crowd had already left.
He had never spoken to the press before that morning.
The editor had just finished when the news broke.
grammar.watch: Only one past perfect is needed to set the scene — the rest of the narrative can stay in the simple past.
grammar.deep: The past perfect exists to establish sequence: it marks the earlier of two past events so that a narrative can move out of chronological order. “By the time the police arrived, the crowd had dispersed” places the dispersal before the arrival without a date. Because its only job is ordering, it becomes optional whenever another word already supplies the order — after, before, then — which is why “After she left, I called” is as correct as “After she had left, I called”. The adverbs that live with it are worth grouping: already, just and never sit between “had” and the participle; yet and by then go to the end; “by the time” and “no sooner … than” introduce the frame. Overusing the tense makes prose heavy, so reserve it for the moments where the sequence genuinely matters.

chart.title: Past perfect and its time adverbs
rows: She had just left when I called.
I had never seen anything like it.
By the time we arrived, it had ended.
No sooner had he sat down than the phone rang.

more: By the time we arrived, the press conference had already finished.
He had never spoken to a journalist before that morning.
The editor had just approved the piece when the lawyers called.
They realised somebody had removed the file.
She hadn’t read the email yet, so she repeated the mistake on air.
Once the story had broken, denial was pointless.

fix.wrong: By the time we arrived, the meeting already finished.
fix.right: By the time we arrived, the meeting had already finished.
fix.why: The earlier of two past events takes the past perfect.

fix.wrong: He had spoke to the press before.
fix.right: He had spoken to the press before.
fix.why: “Had” takes the past participle.

fix.wrong: She had already read it yet.
fix.right: She hadn’t read it yet.
fix.why: “Yet” belongs to negatives and questions; “already” to affirmatives.

drill.name: Which came first
drill.prompt: Join each pair of past events in one sentence, marking the earlier one with the past perfect.
items: the lawyers wrote / the editor apologised
we found the file / they denied it existed
he deleted the account / the reporters noticed

dialogue.line: Why did the editor apologise?
Because by then the paper had already printed it.
Had nobody checked?
The subeditor had just left. The piece went out unread.

contrast.title: Adverb position with the past perfect

grammar.sound: “Had” reduces to /əd/ and clings to the subject: “they’d already gone”. The whole tense can rest on one consonant, so the participle has to do the work.

speaking.text: A journalist interviews an eyewitness, trying to get to the bottom of a confusing story.
This house believes the media blows most stories out of proportion. Agree or disagree.
Tell a partner about a rumour you once heard – what have you found out since?

tips: Use the present perfect (not the past simple) with ‘just, already, yet, ever, never’.
The present perfect continuous stresses duration or that an activity is unfinished.
Common slip: ‘I’ve lived here for five years’ (still here) vs ‘I lived there for five years’ (finished).

quiz.q: Investigators ___ working on the case for months.
quiz.explain: Present perfect continuous (‘have been + -ing’) stresses an ongoing activity over time.

dynamics.name: Front page in ten minutes
dynamics.how: Groups build a front page from six scrambled events, writing the headline in the present perfect and the body in the simple past, with one past-perfect sentence establishing what happened first. Pages are swapped and checked for tense errors.
dynamics.payoff: Newspaper conventions map exactly onto the tense contrast.

dynamics.name: Since or in
dynamics.how: The teacher calls out time expressions; students respond with a full sentence in the correct tense. Any wrong tense passes the turn to the next student.
dynamics.payoff: Automates the signal-word decision at speed.

dynamics.name: Rumour telephone
dynamics.how: A four-sentence story is whispered down the line and written up at the end. The class compares the final version with the original and describes the distortions using perfect tenses.
dynamics.payoff: Produces genuine “has changed / had said” sentences about their own data.

dynamics.name: Interrogate the reporter
dynamics.how: Student A is a reporter who has been covering a story for months; B must ask five questions mixing “Have you…?”, “How long have you been…?” and “What had happened before…?”, and note the tense of each answer.
dynamics.payoff: Question forms are where these tenses collapse, so the drill targets them.

writing.title: A story I followed
writing.brief: Write about a news story you have followed closely. Say what has happened so far, what happened on specific dates, and what had already happened before you started paying attention.
criteria: Three present perfect sentences with unfinished-time or present-result signals.
Three simple past sentences with definite time expressions.
Two past perfect sentences establishing an earlier event, one with already or just.

homework.title: Twelve sentences, three tenses
homework.task: Write four sentences with the present perfect, four with the simple past and four with the past perfect about the same story, underlining the time expression that forces each tense. Then add two present perfect continuous sentences with durations.

test.q: Investigators ___ working on the case for months.
test.explain: An ongoing activity with a duration takes the present perfect continuous.

test.q: The story ___ last night.
test.explain: A definite past time takes the simple past.

test.q: I’ve read ___ articles about it.
test.explain: The simple form counts results.

test.q: By the time we arrived, the press ___ already left.
test.explain: The earlier past event takes the past perfect.

test.q: She hasn’t answered ___ .
test.explain: “Yet” belongs in negatives and questions.

units.title: THE INFORMATION AGE
units.theme: Opinions about technology and its regulation

overview.intro: Giving an opinion in English is rarely a flat statement — it is an invitation. Tag questions and negative questions let you state a view while checking whether the other person shares it, which is exactly what a good discussion needs.
goals: Discuss technology, privacy and information overload with current vocabulary.
Form tag questions correctly, including the tricky auxiliaries.
Use negative questions to soften opinions or express surprise.
Choose between active and passive to hide the agent or emphasise it.
overview.outcome: By the end you can hold a three-minute discussion about technology using at least four tag questions to invite agreement.

vocab.def: to stay informed about, or move at the same pace as, something.
vocab.use: Three parts, so never separable: keep up with the news, keep up with them.
examples: It’s impossible to keep up with every new app.
She struggles to keep up with the rest of the class.
vocab.colloc: keep up with the news · keep up with technology · hard to keep up with

vocab.def: the protection of personal information online.
vocab.use: Uncountable. Common in debates about regulation: data privacy laws, data privacy concerns.
examples: Data privacy is the main worry for most users.
New data privacy rules take effect in January.
vocab.colloc: data privacy laws · data privacy concerns · protect data privacy

vocab.def: too much to deal with; intensely strong.
vocab.use: Two senses: too much (an overwhelming amount) and very strong (overwhelming support). Context decides.
examples: The amount of information online is overwhelming.
There was overwhelming support for the ban.
vocab.colloc: overwhelming amount · overwhelming majority · feel overwhelmed

vocab.def: to disconnect from a device or account.
vocab.use: Also used figuratively for stepping away from the internet entirely. Opposite: log in / log on.
examples: I try to log off completely at weekends.
Remember to log off on shared computers.
vocab.colloc: log off for the day · log off social media

vocab.def: false information that is spread, often unintentionally.
vocab.use: Uncountable. Compare ‘disinformation’, which is false information spread deliberately.
examples: Most misinformation spreads because people share without reading.
Platforms are under pressure to label misinformation.
vocab.colloc: spread misinformation · tackle misinformation · online misinformation

vocab.def: causing a strong urge to keep doing something.
vocab.use: Describes the thing; the person is ‘addicted to’ it. Note the preposition ‘to’ + noun or -ing.
examples: These apps are deliberately addictive.
He’s addicted to checking his notifications.
vocab.colloc: highly addictive · addicted to something · an addictive design

vocab.term: to be glued to a screen
vocab.def: to be unable to stop looking at a device.
vocab.use: Usually with “be”: “The kids are glued to their screens.” Mildly critical.
examples: We were glued to our screens all evening.
He’s glued to his phone at dinner.
vocab.colloc: glued to the screen · glued to your phone

vocab.def: an environment where you only hear opinions like your own.
vocab.use: Common in media discussion: “social media echo chamber”. Countable.
examples: Algorithms create an echo chamber.
We all live in some kind of echo chamber.
vocab.colloc: an online echo chamber · escape the echo chamber

vocab.def: to verify claims before repeating them.
vocab.use: Transitive: “fact-check the story”. Noun: “a fact-check”, “fact-checkers”.
examples: Nobody fact-checked the original post.
I always fact-check before sharing.
vocab.colloc: fact-check a claim · independent fact-checkers

vocab.def: the traceable record you leave online.
vocab.use: Countable, usually singular with a possessive: “your digital footprint”.
examples: Employers look at your digital footprint.
I’d like to shrink my digital footprint.
vocab.colloc: a large digital footprint · leave a digital footprint

vocab.def: to choose not to take part in something you are enrolled in by default.
vocab.use: Intransitive, with “of” before the thing: “opt out of data sharing”. The noun is “an opt-out”.
examples: You can opt out of tracking, but the setting is deliberately hard to find.
Almost nobody opts out, which is the point of the design.
vocab.colloc: opt out of something · an opt-out clause · opt-in by default

vocab.def: to be introduced gradually across a whole system.
vocab.use: Almost always passive, and common in the future passive: “the update will be rolled out next month”.
examples: The new policy is being rolled out region by region.
Facial recognition has already been rolled out at three airports.
vocab.colloc: be rolled out gradually · a phased roll-out

grammar.name: Tag questions
grammar.short: It’s addictive, isn’t it?
grammar.rule: A tag question is a short question added to a statement to invite agreement or confirm information. A positive statement takes a negative tag; a negative statement takes a positive tag.
form: Positive → negative tag: Technology moves fast, doesn’t it?
Negative → positive tag: You haven’t logged off, have you?
The tag repeats the auxiliary; with no auxiliary, use do / does / did.
notes: The pronoun in the tag matches the subject: ‘Your phone is old, isn’t it?’
Falling intonation on the tag means you expect agreement; rising intonation makes it a genuine question.
Special cases: ‘I’m right, aren’t I?’, ‘Let’s go, shall we?’, ‘Open the window, will you?’
examples: Technology moves fast, doesn’t it?
You’ve seen the new update, haven’t you?
Nobody reads the terms, do they?
grammar.watch: Match the tag to the auxiliary, not to the meaning: ‘This app collects data, doesn’t it?’ — not ‘isn’t it?’
grammar.deep: A tag question turns a statement into a check, and its grammar is mechanical: repeat the auxiliary, reverse the polarity, and use a pronoun. Positive statements take negative tags (“You’ve seen it, haven’t you?”), negative statements take positive tags (“You haven’t seen it, have you?”). When the statement has no auxiliary, “do” stands in. What learners underestimate is intonation, because it changes the function entirely: falling intonation asks for agreement and expects a yes, while rising intonation is a genuine question. A handful of irregular tags repay memorising — “I’m late, aren’t I?”, “Let’s go, shall we?”, “Open the window, will you?”, “Nobody called, did they?” — and note that indefinite pronouns like nobody and everyone take “they” in the tag regardless of their singular verb.
more: This app collects location data, doesn’t it?
You haven’t read the terms, have you?
Nobody actually reads them, do they?
Let’s turn the notifications off, shall we?
There’s no way to delete the account, is there?
I’m being paranoid, aren’t I?

fix.wrong: This app collects data, isn’t it?
fix.right: This app collects data, doesn’t it?
fix.why: The tag repeats the auxiliary of the statement, and “collects” needs “do”.

fix.wrong: Nobody reads the terms, don’t they?
fix.right: Nobody reads the terms, do they?
fix.why: “Nobody” makes the statement negative, so the tag is positive.

fix.wrong: I’m late, amn’t I?
fix.right: I’m late, aren’t I?
fix.why: English has no contraction for “am not” in tags; “aren’t I” is the fixed form.

drill.name: Tag it
drill.prompt: Add the correct tag to each statement, then say it twice — once to check information, once to invite agreement.
items: There aren’t any settings for that

dialogue.line: You’ve turned off location, haven’t you?
I thought I had. It resets after every update, doesn’t it?
Apparently. Nobody mentions that, do they?
Let’s check the settings again, shall we?

grammar.sound: A falling tag invites agreement; a rising tag asks a real question. Said flat, the tag sounds sarcastic, which is why intonation matters more here than the grammar.

grammar.name: Negative questions for opinions
grammar.short: Isn’t it worrying how much they collect?
grammar.rule: A negative question is not really asking for information. It either expresses surprise, invites agreement, or softens a strong opinion into something more sociable.
form: Isn’t it + adjective + clause: Isn’t it amazing how fast things change?
Don’t you think + clause: Don’t you think we should log off more?
Haven’t / Didn’t + subject: Haven’t you read the privacy policy?
notes: Answering can be confusing: ‘Don’t you agree?’ — ‘Yes’ means you do agree.
Used with strong stress, a negative question can sound like criticism: ‘Didn’t you check?’
The contracted form is far more natural in speech than ‘Do you not think…?’, which sounds formal or annoyed.
examples: Isn’t it worrying how much data they collect?
Don’t you think children get phones too early?
Haven’t we all shared something without checking it?
grammar.watch: Use the contraction at the front — ‘Isn’t it…?’, not ‘Is not it…?’
grammar.deep: Negative questions are not simply questions with “not” in them; they carry an expectation. “Didn’t you send it?” signals that you believed it had been sent and are now surprised — which makes the form useful for polite pressure and dangerous for accidental accusation. In opinion-giving, the same structure invites agreement: “Isn’t it strange that nobody complained?” asks the listener to share your reaction rather than to supply information. Two mechanics matter. Contractions are normal in speech and the uncontracted form (“Did you not send it?”) is markedly formal or annoyed. And the answers are famously slippery: to “Didn’t you send it?”, a bare “yes” means you did send it, and English speakers usually add the verb — “Yes, I did” or “No, I didn’t” — precisely to remove the ambiguity.

chart.title: Negative questions for opinions
rows: Don’t you think it’s too soon?
Wouldn’t it be better to wait?
No, I haven’t. / Yes, I have.

more: Isn’t it strange how quickly we accepted all this?
Don’t you think fourteen is too young for an unfiltered feed?
Haven’t we all clicked “accept” without reading?
Wouldn’t it make more sense to ask permission first?
Didn’t they promise the data would stay in the country?
Isn’t there anyone who checks these claims?

fix.wrong: Is not it worrying?
fix.right: Isn’t it worrying?
fix.why: The negative question uses the contraction at the front.

fix.wrong: Don’t you think that is it too young?
fix.right: Don’t you think fourteen is too young?
fix.why: The clause after “think” keeps statement word order.

fix.wrong: Isn’t it worrying how much data do they collect?
fix.right: Isn’t it worrying how much data they collect?
fix.why: An embedded question is not inverted.

drill.name: Soften the opinion
drill.prompt: Turn each blunt opinion into a negative question, then say whether you are inviting agreement or expressing surprise.

dialogue.line: Don’t you think the rules are far too weak?
Weak, or just unenforced?
Isn’t that the same thing in practice?
Haven’t we been having this argument for ten years?

contrast.title: Negative question, which function
rows: Isn’t it amazing how fast it changed?
Don’t you think it’s too much?
Wouldn’t it be simpler to ask?

grammar.sound: The stress sits on the adjective or the main verb, not on the negative: “isn’t it WORrying”. Stressing “isn’t” turns an invitation into a challenge.

grammar.name: Passive of present continuous, present perfect, future
grammar.short: Hide the agent, or bring it back for emphasis.
grammar.rule: If the agent (the person or thing doing the action) is unknown or obvious from the context, it’s better to use a passive form. However, if the person or thing doing the action needs to be emphasized, it’s better to use an active form.
form: Present continuous passive: am / is / are + being + past participle — The spyware is being used to collect information.
Present perfect passive: have / has + been + past participle — Social networking sites have been used in criminal investigations.
Future passive: will be / is going to be + past participle — The new privacy rules will be announced next month.
notes: The passive is very rarely used with the present perfect continuous. Use the passive of the present perfect instead: ‘More videos have been posted to the Internet this year than ever before.’
Keep the active when the agent is the news: ‘A criminal organization has created this virus, not an amateur hacker.’
Add ‘by + agent’ only when the agent is new or surprising information — otherwise leave it out completely.
In the future passive, only ‘be’ changes: will be collected, is going to be collected, will have been collected.
examples: The spyware is being used to collect information about college students. (Agent is unknown.)
Social networking sites have been used in criminal investigations. (Agent is clear from context.)
A criminal organization has created this virus, not an amateur hacker. (Agent is emphasized.)
People have been posting more videos to the Internet this year than ever before. → More videos have been posted to the Internet this year than ever before.
Millions of accounts are going to be checked before the new rules take effect.
grammar.watch: Never write ‘have been being posted’ — the present perfect continuous has no natural passive. Use the present perfect passive.
grammar.deep: The passive is not a politeness device and not a way of sounding academic; it is a way of choosing what the sentence starts with. English sentences put the known, the given or the topic first, so when the agent is unknown, irrelevant or already obvious, the passive lets the affected thing take the subject position: ‘The spyware is being used to collect information.’ Nobody knows who wrote the spyware, and the sentence does not pretend otherwise. When the agent is the point — the whole reason the sentence exists — the active form must come back, which is why ‘A criminal organization has created this virus, not an amateur hacker’ cannot be passive without losing its argument. Mechanically, each tense keeps its own auxiliaries and adds ‘be’ plus the past participle: the present continuous inserts ‘being’ (is being used), the present perfect inserts ‘been’ (has been used), and future forms simply add ‘be’ after the future marker (will be used, is going to be used). The one gap in the system is the present perfect continuous: ‘has been being used’ is grammatically derivable but nobody says it, so English uses the present perfect passive instead and lets the context supply the sense of ongoing activity. In writing about technology, research and regulation, this pattern does most of the work: processes and data take the subject position, and the agent appears only when naming it changes the reader’s conclusion.

chart.title: Passive across the tenses
rows: The spyware is being used to collect data.
Two accounts have been suspended today.
The report will be published on Monday.
is / are going to be + p.p.
New rules are going to be introduced.
By June the app will have been removed.
avoid — use the present perfect passive
More videos have been posted than ever before.
by + agent, only when it is news
This virus was created by a criminal organization.

more: Facial recognition is being tested in two stations.
Three million accounts have been closed since the rule changed.
The rest of the update will be rolled out in April.
Nothing has been explained to the users.
Data is being collected while the app sits in the background.
The report will have been published by the time we meet.

fix.wrong: The spyware is used to collect information right now.
fix.right: The spyware is being used to collect information right now.
fix.why: An action in progress takes the continuous passive.

fix.wrong: Three accounts have been close.
fix.right: Three accounts have been closed.
fix.why: The passive needs the past participle after “been”.

fix.wrong: The update will roll out next month by the company.
fix.right: The update will be rolled out next month by the company.
fix.why: With the agent named at the end, the verb must be passive.

drill.name: Hide the agent, then bring it back
drill.prompt: Say each fact twice: once as a passive with no agent, once with the agent restored for emphasis.

dialogue.line: Has anything actually been done?
Two features have been withdrawn.
And the tracking?
It’s still being tested. We’re told the results will be published in the autumn.

grammar.sound: “Been” and “be” are unstressed, so the pair “is being tested” compresses to /ɪz bɪɪŋ ˈtestid/. The stress falls on the participle, which is the word carrying the news.

speaking.text: Two friends argue about whether children should have smartphones – use tag questions to seek agreement.
This house believes social media should be regulated like other media. Argue for or against.
Ask your partner three tag questions about their tech habits, then react to the answers.

tips: A positive statement takes a negative tag, and vice versa: ‘It works, doesn’t it?’ / ‘It doesn’t work, does it?’
The tag repeats the auxiliary; if there’s none, use ‘do / does / did’.
Common slip: the tag for ‘I am’ is ‘aren’t I?’ – ‘I’m right, aren’t I?’

quiz.q: This app collects a lot of data, ___?
quiz.explain: A positive statement with ‘collects’ takes the negative tag ‘doesn’t it’.

dynamics.name: Terms and conditions read-aloud
dynamics.how: Groups rewrite a real clause from an app’s terms into plain English using passives, then present both versions. The class votes on which passive hid the most.
dynamics.payoff: Makes the agent-hiding function of the passive concrete rather than abstract.

dynamics.name: Tag ping-pong
dynamics.how: Student A makes a statement about technology, B adds the tag and answers it, then reverses roles. Ten rounds each, and any mismatched auxiliary ends the round.
dynamics.payoff: Speed removes the time to translate, which is where tags go wrong.

dynamics.name: The regulator
dynamics.how: Two students defend a tech product, three act as regulators using only negative questions to attack it. The defenders must answer without repeating a phrase.
dynamics.payoff: Negative questions are a debating tool, so a debate is the natural drill.

dynamics.name: Rewrite the announcement
dynamics.how: Pairs receive an active corporate announcement and rewrite it entirely in the passive, then decide which sentences became less honest and mark them.
dynamics.payoff: Links grammar choice to ethics, which fixes it in memory.

writing.title: One thing about technology that worries me
writing.brief: Write about one technology you use and distrust. Describe what is being done with your data using passive forms, and use tag questions or negative questions at least twice to bring the reader onto your side.
criteria: Four passives across at least three different tenses, one with the agent named.
Two negative questions or tag questions with correct auxiliaries.
No inverted word order in an embedded question.

homework.title: Ten tags, six passives
homework.task: Write ten statements about technology and add the correct tag to each, marking whether you would say it with rising or falling intonation. Then write six passive sentences — two present continuous, two present perfect, two future — and name the agent in only two of them.

test.q: This app collects a lot of data, ___?
test.explain: The tag repeats the auxiliary, and “collects” needs “do”.

test.q: Nobody reads the terms, ___?
test.explain: “Nobody” makes the statement negative, so the tag is positive.

test.q: ___ it worrying how much they know?
test.explain: Negative questions use the front contraction.

test.q: The software ___ tested in two cities at the moment.
test.explain: An action in progress takes “is being + participle”.

test.q: The update ___ rolled out next month.
test.explain: The future passive is “will be + past participle”.

units.title: PUTTING THE MIND TO WORK
units.theme: Psychology, memory and how the brain works

overview.intro: Writing about how the mind works means packing information densely. Reduced relative clauses let you cut words without losing meaning, and sentence-modifying ‘which’ lets you comment on a whole idea — both are hallmarks of B2 writing.
goals: Talk about memory, forgetting and mental effort with idiomatic language.
Shorten relative clauses by removing the pronoun and ‘be’.
Comment on a whole clause using non-defining ‘, which…’.
overview.outcome: By the end you can explain a memory technique in writing, using two reduced relative clauses and one sentence-modifying ‘which’.

vocab.def: to be forgotten.
vocab.use: The forgotten thing is the subject: ‘It slipped my mind’, not ‘I slipped my mind’. A soft, polite excuse.
examples: Sorry, your birthday completely slipped my mind.
The appointment slipped his mind until the reminder arrived.
vocab.colloc: it slipped my mind · completely slip your mind

vocab.def: to think very hard to remember or solve something.
vocab.use: Often followed by ‘trying to’ or ‘for’: racking my brains for a name.
examples: I racked my brains but couldn’t remember where we’d met.
We racked our brains trying to solve the last clue.
vocab.colloc: rack your brains for something · rack your brains trying to…

vocab.def: producing powerful, clear images in the mind.
vocab.use: Used of memories, dreams, descriptions and colours. Strongly positive when describing writing.
examples: I have a vivid memory of my first day at school.
She gave a vivid description of the accident.
vocab.colloc: a vivid memory · a vivid dream · vivid detail

vocab.def: to help someone remember something.
vocab.use: Something external does the jogging: a photo, a smell, a question.
examples: Maybe this photo will jog your memory.
He mentioned the hotel name to jog my memory.
vocab.colloc: jog someone’s memory · something to jog your memory

vocab.def: forgetful because your thoughts are elsewhere.
vocab.use: Gentle and often affectionate — it suggests a thinker, not a careless person.
examples: My absent-minded uncle once left the car keys in the fridge.
I’ve been so absent-minded this week.
vocab.colloc: an absent-minded professor · rather absent-minded

vocab.def: (of information) to be fully understood or realised.
vocab.use: Intransitive and always about news or facts, usually with a delay: ‘It hasn’t sunk in yet.’
examples: It took a day for the news to sink in.
I heard the result, but it still hasn’t sunk in.
vocab.colloc: take time to sink in · hasn’t sunk in yet · slowly sink in

vocab.def: to be unable to remember or find something.
vocab.use: No object: “I asked him the date and he drew a blank.”
examples: I drew a blank on her surname.
We drew a blank at the archive.
vocab.colloc: draw a complete blank

vocab.term: on the tip of my tongue
vocab.def: almost remembered but not quite.
vocab.use: Fixed phrase with “be”: “Her name is on the tip of my tongue.”
examples: It’s on the tip of my tongue — give me a second.
The word was on the tip of my tongue all morning.
vocab.colloc: on the tip of my tongue

vocab.def: to think about something slowly and carefully.
vocab.use: Separable: “mull it over”, “mull over the offer”.
examples: Let me mull it over and get back to you.
She mulled over the decision for a week.
vocab.colloc: mull it over · mull over an offer

vocab.def: the ability to keep information in memory.
vocab.use: Uncountable in this sense: “memory retention”, “poor retention”. Also used about staff and customers.
examples: Sleep improves retention.
Retention drops without revision.
vocab.colloc: memory retention · improve retention

vocab.def: to understand something difficult, often suddenly.
vocab.use: Transitive, slightly formal: “grasp the concept”. “Get your head around” is the informal equivalent.
examples: It took me a term to grasp what the experiment actually proved.
Some students grasp it immediately and can’t explain why.
vocab.colloc: grasp a concept · fully grasp · hard to grasp

vocab.def: to have a natural skill for something.
vocab.use: Followed by a noun or a gerund: “a knack for remembering names”.
examples: She has a knack for explaining statistics without slides.
He’s got a knack for finding the flaw in any argument.
vocab.colloc: a knack for something · quite a knack

grammar.name: Reduced relative clauses
grammar.short: the woman who is standing → the woman standing.
grammar.rule: When a relative clause contains a form of ‘be’, you can delete the relative pronoun and ‘be’ together. When it contains an active verb, you can replace the pronoun and verb with an -ing form.
form: Active → -ing: The people who were waiting outside → the people waiting outside.
Passive → past participle: The study that was published → the study published.
With a general subject: Anyone who wants to join → anyone wanting to join.
notes: Only defining relative clauses are normally reduced in everyday English.
A reduced clause keeps its position immediately after the noun it describes.
The reduction works only when the relative pronoun is the SUBJECT of the clause — ‘the book that I read’ cannot become ‘the book reading’.
examples: The people waiting outside were all volunteers.
The technique used by the researchers is surprisingly simple.
Anyone wanting to join should sign up today.
grammar.watch: Never reduce when the pronoun is the object of the clause — it changes who is doing the action.
grammar.deep: Reduced relative clauses drop the relative pronoun and the form of “be”, leaving a participle to modify the noun directly: “the students who are waiting outside” becomes “the students waiting outside”, and “the report that was written by the auditor” becomes “the report written by the auditor”. The present participle carries active meaning, the past participle passive, which makes the pair a compact way to add information without an extra clause. Written English relies on this heavily, so learning to produce it is one of the fastest ways to raise your register. The constraint is that the reduction is only available when the clause contains “be” plus a participle or when the verb can be expressed as a participle — you cannot reduce “the man who owns the café”, since there is no participle available.

chart.title: Reducing relative clauses
rows: the woman who lives next door
a decision that was taken in May
the man who owns the café

more: The students taking part were paid nothing.
Anyone wanting to volunteer should email the lab.
The technique used in the 1970s has been abandoned.
The results published last week contradict the earlier study.
A theory built on twelve participants proves very little.
The part of the brain responsible for faces is surprisingly small.

fix.wrong: The study was published contradicts the theory.
fix.right: The study published contradicts the theory.
fix.why: The reduced form deletes the relative pronoun and “be” together — you cannot keep “was”.

fix.wrong: The people waited outside were volunteers.
fix.right: The people waiting outside were volunteers.
fix.why: An active clause reduces to -ing; the past participle would make them the object.

fix.wrong: The researcher who I met her yesterday published it.
fix.right: The researcher I met yesterday published it.
fix.why: An object pronoun can be dropped, but the object cannot be repeated.

drill.name: Cut it down
drill.prompt: Reduce each relative clause, or say why it cannot be reduced.
items: the participants who were waiting in the corridor
the method that was used in the study
the theory which explains the effect
anyone who wants to take part

dialogue.line: Which study do you mean?
The one published in March.
With the students taking part for free?
That’s the one. Anyone reading it carefully spots the problem.

grammar.sound: The reduced phrase runs straight onto the noun with no pause: “the study PUBlished in March”. A pause in that gap makes listeners hear a full clause and wait for a verb that never comes.

grammar.name: Sentence-modifying ‘which’
grammar.short: He forgot my name, which was embarrassing.
grammar.rule: After a comma, ‘which’ can refer back to the whole preceding idea rather than to a single noun, letting you add a comment or reaction.
form: , which + verb + comment: She solved it in seconds, which impressed everyone.
, which is / was + adjective: He forgot my name, which was embarrassing.
Can end the sentence: They cancelled the study, which surprised no one.
notes: The comma is obligatory — without it, ‘which’ seems to refer only to the nearest noun.
This structure is a favourite in written commentary and reviews.
It cannot start a new sentence in formal writing: join it to the clause it comments on.
examples: She solved it in seconds, which impressed everyone.
They cancelled the study, which surprised no one.
He remembered every detail, which is unusual after so long.
grammar.watch: Use ‘, which’, never ‘what’ or ‘that’, to comment on a whole clause.
grammar.deep: “Which” can refer not to a noun but to the whole preceding clause, adding your comment on the situation: “She resigned without notice, which surprised everyone.” The comma is obligatory, because this is by definition non-defining information, and “that” is impossible. This structure is how English attaches evaluation to a fact in a single sentence, and it is extremely common in speech and journalism. Two cautions. Keep the reference unambiguous: if the sentence contains several nouns, a reader may attach “which” to the nearest one, so consider “a fact which” or “something that” to disambiguate. And avoid stacking two of them; a sentence with two sentence-modifying clauses collapses under its own commentary. In more formal writing the same job is done by “, a development which…” or “, thereby…”.

chart.title: Sentence-modifying which
rows: He arrived late, which annoyed the client.
She never replied, which is why I called.
Sales fell, which means we cut costs.
He was late, that annoyed us. ✘
He denied it, a fact which surprised nobody.
no comma, refers to a noun

more: She solved it in under a minute, which impressed everyone.
He forgot the whole talk, which was awkward for all of us.
The funding ran out in March, which explains the small sample.
They tested only students, which limits the conclusion badly.
Nobody replicated the result, which should have ended the debate.
The paper was withdrawn, which almost never happens.

fix.wrong: She solved it in seconds, that impressed everyone.
fix.right: She solved it in seconds, which impressed everyone.
fix.why: Only “which” can refer back to a whole idea.

fix.wrong: He forgot my name, what was embarrassing.
fix.right: He forgot my name, which was embarrassing.
fix.why: “What” cannot introduce a non-defining clause.

fix.wrong: They cancelled the study which was unexpected.
fix.right: They cancelled the study, which was unexpected.
fix.why: Without the comma the clause defines the study instead of commenting on the event.

drill.name: Add the comment
drill.prompt: Finish each statement with “, which…”, commenting on the whole idea rather than the last noun.
items: The experiment was repeated three times
She remembered every name in the room
The data was lost in a software update
The results were published without review

dialogue.line: They ran the whole study on forty students.
Which tells you almost nothing about anyone else.
And it was never replicated.
Which is the part that worries me, honestly.

contrast.title: which, that, or what
rows: She left early, which surprised us.
What surprised us was the delay.

grammar.sound: There is a real pause before the comment clause and the pitch drops on it, which is how listeners know the “which” refers to everything and not to the last noun.

speaking.text: A memory trainer teaches a client a technique – explain the steps and answer their questions.
This house believes we rely on our phones too much and it’s ruining our memory. Agree or disagree.
Share a memory trick you use, then describe a time something completely slipped your mind.

tips: You can reduce a relative clause when it contains a form of ‘be’ or an active -ing action.
Sentence-modifying ‘which’ always follows a comma and refers to the whole previous idea.
Common slip: don’t use ‘what’ to comment on a whole clause – use ‘, which’.

quiz.q: The results, ___ surprised the whole team, were published today.
quiz.explain: A non-defining clause commenting on the whole idea uses ‘, which’.

dynamics.name: Caption the experiment
dynamics.how: Pairs receive four descriptions of psychology experiments and must compress each into a single noun phrase with a reduced relative clause, then read them aloud for the class to expand back into full clauses.
dynamics.payoff: Compression and expansion in the same activity makes the transformation visible.

dynamics.name: Which-chain
dynamics.how: One student states a fact; the next adds “, which…” commenting on it, and the next comments on that. The chain must survive six links without repeating a comment adjective.
dynamics.payoff: Trains the whole-idea reference that learners default to “that” for.

dynamics.name: Memory test, then report
dynamics.how: Groups run a sixty-second memory test on each other, then write four sentences reporting the results, each containing a reduced relative clause and one “, which” comment.
dynamics.payoff: Their own data gives them something worth commenting on.

dynamics.name: Spot the dangler
dynamics.how: Pairs receive ten sentences, half with illegal reductions, and must mark and repair the broken ones, explaining who is doing what in each.
dynamics.payoff: Error-spotting is faster than production for this particular rule.

writing.title: Something my memory does badly
writing.brief: Describe a way your own memory fails — names, faces, directions, numbers. Use reduced relative clauses to pack in detail, and comment on at least two of your own statements with “, which…”.
criteria: Four reduced relative clauses, at least one passive and one active.
Two sentence-modifying “which” clauses, correctly punctuated.
No repeated object pronoun inside a relative clause.

homework.title: Reduce eight, comment on five
homework.task: Write eight sentences with full relative clauses about how the mind works, then rewrite each in reduced form, marking any that cannot be reduced. Add five statements each followed by a “, which…” comment.

test.q: The results, ___ surprised the whole team, were published today.
test.explain: A clause commenting on the whole idea uses “, which”.

test.q: The people ___ outside were all volunteers.
test.explain: An active clause reduces to the -ing form.

test.q: The technique ___ by the researchers is very simple.
test.explain: A passive clause reduces to the past participle.

test.q: Which sentence is correct?
options: Anyone wanting to join should sign up.
Anyone wanted to join should sign up.
Anyone who wanting to join should sign up.
test.explain: “Who wants” reduces to “wanting”.

test.q: She solved it in seconds, ___ impressed everyone.
test.explain: Only “which” can refer back to a whole clause.

Under it, two arrows: ACTIVE → -ING and PASSIVE → PAST PARTICIPLE.
A red box: “The people waited outside” with an arrow to “who waited them?”
