units.title: GENERALLY SPEAKING

overview.intro: Talking about cultures means generalising — and generalising safely means signalling the exceptions. This unit gives you contrast structures for comparing groups, and the two past-habit forms for describing how things used to be.
goals: Discuss customs, norms and stereotypes without overgeneralising.
Contrast and except with unlike, while, whereas and except that.
Describe past habits and states with ‘used to’ and ‘would’.
overview.outcome: By the end you can compare two cultures you know using three contrast structures, and describe how your own habits used to be different.

vocab.def: an oversimplified, fixed idea about a group of people.
vocab.use: Nearly always negative. As a verb: ‘to stereotype someone’. The adjective is ‘stereotypical’.
examples: The film relies on tired national stereotypes.
It’s unfair to stereotype an entire generation.
vocab.colloc: a common stereotype · challenge a stereotype · stereotypical behaviour

vocab.def: to make a broad statement that may not fit every case.
vocab.use: Often self-critical: ‘I’m generalising, but…’ — a useful hedge in a debate.
examples: I’m generalising, but people here tend to eat later.
It’s risky to generalise from a single visit.
vocab.colloc: generalise about something · a sweeping generalisation

vocab.def: a standard or typical pattern of behaviour in a society.
vocab.use: Countable (social norms) and also in the phrase ‘the norm’ meaning the usual thing.
examples: Working from home has become the norm here.
Social norms around punctuality vary enormously.
vocab.colloc: social norms · cultural norms · become the norm

vocab.def: the way a person is raised as a child.
vocab.use: Almost always singular with a possessive: my upbringing, a strict upbringing.
examples: She had a very strict upbringing in a small town.
My upbringing taught me to greet everyone in the room.
vocab.colloc: a strict / religious / traditional upbringing

vocab.def: to feel accepted and comfortable within a group.
vocab.use: Use ‘with’ for the group: fit in with the others. Not separable.
examples: It took a year to fit in at my new school.
He never quite fitted in with the rest of the team.
vocab.colloc: fit in with a group · struggle to fit in · fit right in

vocab.def: traditional ways of behaving in a particular culture.
vocab.use: In the plural for traditions; the singular ‘customs’ at an airport is a different word entirely.
examples: Local customs vary from one region to the next.
It’s polite to learn a few customs before you travel.
vocab.colloc: local customs · traditional customs · respect the customs

vocab.term: to paint with a broad brush
vocab.def: to describe a group without noticing differences.
vocab.use: Often critical: “That’s painting with a very broad brush.”
examples: It’s painting with a broad brush to say all young people are online all day.
I don’t want to paint with too broad a brush.
vocab.colloc: paint with a broad brush

vocab.def: firmly established and hard to change.
vocab.use: With abstract nouns: “deep-rooted beliefs”, “deep-rooted prejudice”. Also “deeply rooted”.
examples: These customs are deep-rooted.
The habit is too deep-rooted to break quickly.
vocab.colloc: deep-rooted beliefs · deep-rooted problem

vocab.def: to behave the way a group expects.
vocab.use: “Conform to + norms / standards”: “conform to expectations”. Noun: conformity.
examples: Teenagers feel pressure to conform.
The design must conform to safety standards.
vocab.colloc: conform to norms · pressure to conform

vocab.def: generally, with some exceptions.
vocab.use: A hedge for generalisations, usually at the start: “By and large, people were supportive.”
examples: By and large, the system works.
By and large, they kept their promises.
vocab.colloc: by and large · on the whole

grammar.name: Contrast and exception
grammar.short: unlike / while / whereas / except that.
grammar.rule: These structures set two ideas against each other. Choosing the right one depends on whether you are contrasting nouns, contrasting whole clauses, or noting a single exception.
form: unlike + noun: Unlike my brother, I love mornings.
while / whereas + clause: While some cultures value punctuality, others are more relaxed.
except (that) + clause / except for + noun: It’s a great city, except that it rains a lot.
notes: ‘Whereas’ is more formal than ‘while’ and only ever means contrast — ‘while’ can also mean ‘during’.
‘Unlike’ must be followed by a noun or pronoun, never a clause.
‘Except for’ introduces the one thing that spoils an otherwise complete statement.
examples: Unlike my brother, I love getting up early.
While some cultures value punctuality, others are far more relaxed.
The trip was perfect, except for the flight home.
grammar.watch: To contrast two full clauses use ‘while’ or ‘whereas’ — ‘unlike’ only compares nouns.
grammar.deep: Contrast and exception are distinct moves, and B2 writing needs both. Contrast sets two ideas side by side — while, whereas, on the other hand, in contrast — and both halves stay true. Exception removes a case from a generalisation — except (for), apart from, other than, with the exception of, unless — and here the grammar is stricter: “except for” takes a noun, “except that” takes a clause, and “unless” takes a conditional clause. This pairing is what lets you hedge honestly: state the general rule, then name the exception, and your claim becomes defensible instead of absolute. In academic register the same work is done by “notwithstanding”, “albeit” and “save for”, but the everyday set is enough for most writing, and mixing categories — “despite it rained”, “except it was late” — is the error to watch.

chart.title: Contrast and exception
rows: Bogotá is cool, whereas Cali is hot.
By contrast, sales rose in March.
It’s perfect, except that it’s expensive.
There’s nothing to do other than wait.
Nobody leaves unless I say so.

more: Unlike my colleagues in Bogotá, the Madrid team eats lunch at three.
While punctuality matters here, nobody expects it socially.
Whereas older relatives phone, my cousins send voice notes and nothing else.
Everyone brings something, except that nobody brings dessert.
People here are formal at work but not at all formal afterwards.
In contrast to what visitors expect, the city is quiet by eleven.

fix.wrong: Unlike in my country people eat late.
fix.right: Unlike in my country, people here eat late.
fix.why: “Unlike” introduces a phrase that needs a comma and a contrasting main clause.

fix.wrong: Whereas the north is colder than the south is warmer.
fix.right: The north is colder, whereas the south is warmer.
fix.why: “Whereas” joins two full clauses and only one of them carries it.

fix.wrong: Everyone came except that Marta.
fix.right: Everyone came except Marta.
fix.why: “Except that” introduces a clause; before a noun use “except”.

drill.name: Two cultures, one sentence
drill.prompt: Contrast the two habits in one sentence, using a different connector each time.
items: lunch at one / lunch at three
dinner guests arrive early / arrive late

dialogue.line: Is eight o’clock too early for dinner?
Here, yes. Unlike in London, nobody eats before nine.
So what do people do until then?
Whereas you’d go home, everyone here stays out. Except that nobody calls it dinner.

contrast.title: Contrast and exception
rows: While she cooks, he orders in.

grammar.sound: “Whereas” carries the stress on the second syllable, /weəˈræz/, and the clause before it ends on a small rise. Flattening that rise makes the two halves sound unrelated.

grammar.name: Past habits: used to and would
grammar.short: States take ‘used to’; repeated actions take either.
grammar.rule: ‘Used to’ describes past states and repeated actions that are no longer true. ‘Would’ describes repeated past actions only — never states.
form: used to + base verb: We used to live in a small town.
would + base verb: Every summer, my grandmother would tell us stories.
Negative and question: didn’t use to · Did you use to…?
notes: States (be, have, know, live, like) work only with ‘used to’: ‘I used to be shy’, not ‘I would be shy’.
‘Would’ needs a past time frame already established, which is why it is common in storytelling.
Don’t confuse ‘used to do’ (past habit) with ‘be used to doing’ (be accustomed to).
examples: We used to live by the sea.
Every summer, my grandmother would tell us the same story.
I didn’t use to like coffee at all.
grammar.watch: In negatives and questions the ‘d’ disappears: ‘Did you use to…?’, not ‘Did you used to…?’
grammar.deep: “Used to” and “would” both describe the past habitually, but they are not interchangeable. “Used to” covers repeated actions and long-term states: “We used to live in Pasto”, “She used to be shy”. “Would” covers repeated actions only, and it needs an established past frame to work in, which is why storytelling favours it: “Every August we would drive to the coast.” Putting “would” with a state produces nonsense — “She would be shy” shifts into the conditional. Two extra notes. Both structures imply the habit has stopped, so they are inherently contrastive; and the past simple can do the same job when a frequency phrase carries the repetition (“we drove there every August”), which is often the lighter option. Negatives and questions are formed with “didn’t use to” and “Did you use to…?”, with no final -d.

chart.title: Used to vs would for past habits

more: We used to eat together every Sunday, and nobody asked why.
My grandmother would tell the same three stories at every meal.
I didn’t use to like coffee; now I can’t start without it.
There used to be a market where the car park is.
Every summer we would drive nine hours and complain the whole way.
We used to be the family that arrived early. That changed.

fix.wrong: I would live in Cali as a child.
fix.right: I used to live in Cali as a child.
fix.why: “Would” cannot express a past state; only “used to” can.

fix.wrong: I didn’t used to like it.
fix.right: I didn’t use to like it.
fix.why: After the auxiliary “did” the base form “use” is required.

fix.wrong: We use to go every summer.
fix.right: We used to go every summer.
fix.why: The form is fixed in the past: “used to”.

drill.name: State or action
drill.prompt: For each item, say whether it is a state or a repeated action, then use the correct form — or both if both are possible.
items: spend every August at the coast

dialogue.line: Did your family eat together when you were small?
Every Sunday. My aunt would arrive an hour late every single time.
And now?
There used to be twelve of us. Now there are four, and nobody is late.

grammar.sound: “Used to” is one word in speech, /ˈjuːstə/, with no /d/ audible. The written “didn’t used to” exists because nobody can hear the difference.

speaking.text: Two travellers compare culture-shock stories from different countries they’ve visited.
This house believes stereotypes always contain a grain of truth. Agree or disagree.
Describe a childhood habit using ‘used to’ and ‘would’ – and whether you’ve grown out of it.

tips: Use ‘would’ for repeated past actions, but ‘used to’ for past states: ‘I used to be shy’, not ‘I would be shy’.
In the negative and question, drop the -d: ‘didn’t use to’, ‘Did you use to…?’
Common slip: ‘unlike’ compares nouns; to contrast whole clauses use ‘while’ or ‘whereas’.

quiz.q: When I was a child, we ___ live by the sea.
quiz.explain: For a past state (living somewhere), use ‘used to’, not ‘would’.

dynamics.name: Generalisation hedge
dynamics.how: Student A makes a blunt cultural generalisation; B repeats it hedged with “by and large”, “as a rule” or “tends to”, then adds an exception with “except that”. Ten rounds, then swap.
dynamics.payoff: Pairs the structure with the social skill it exists for.

dynamics.name: Then and now boards
dynamics.how: Groups draw two columns for their childhood and now, fill six lines each, then present using “used to” for states and “would” for repeated actions. Listeners challenge any “would” with a state verb.
dynamics.payoff: The challenge rule teaches the one restriction that matters.

dynamics.name: Culture shock panel
dynamics.how: Each student describes a habit that surprised them somewhere else, using a contrast connector, and the group finds the counter-example. No generalisation may stand unchallenged.
dynamics.payoff: Contrast connectors get used where they belong — in argument.

dynamics.name: Wouldn’t or didn’t
dynamics.how: The teacher reads past habits at speed; students must produce the negative in the right form. Any “didn’t used to” passes the turn.
dynamics.payoff: Isolates the spelling-and-sound trap directly.

writing.title: What visitors get wrong about where I live
writing.brief: Describe two or three assumptions outsiders make about your city or country, contrasting each with what actually happens. Include a paragraph on how these habits have changed since your childhood.
criteria: Four contrast connectors, each followed by the right structure.
Three past-habit forms, using “would” only for repeated actions.
Two hedges so that no generalisation is stated as absolute.

homework.title: Six contrasts, six habits
homework.task: Write six sentences contrasting two places you know, using unlike, while, whereas, except that, apart from and but once each. Then write six past-habit sentences, marking each as a state or a repeated action.

test.q: ___ my parents, I can’t sleep before midnight.
test.explain: “Unlike” is followed by a noun phrase.

test.q: The north is colder, ___ the south stays mild.
test.explain: “Whereas” joins two full clauses.

test.q: I ___ live in a much smaller town.
test.explain: A past state takes “used to” only.

test.q: My grandmother ___ tell the same story every Sunday.
test.explain: A repeated past action allows “would”.

test.q: I ___ like coffee at all.
test.explain: After “did” the base form “use” is required.

board: Top left: UNLIKE / IN CONTRAST TO + noun, and WHILE / WHEREAS + clause, each with an example.
Top right: EXCEPT + noun and EXCEPT THAT + clause, with a crossed-out “except that Marta”.
Centre: two columns headed STATES and REPEATED ACTIONS, with USED TO written across both and WOULD only over the right-hand one.
A red box: “I would live in Cali as a child” with WOULD crossed out.

units.title: THE ART OF COMPLAINING

overview.intro: Complaining in a second language is risky: too soft and nothing happens, too direct and you sound aggressive. Indirect questions and noun clauses give you the distance that English politeness relies on.
goals: Describe faults, annoyances and solutions with the right register.
Use noun clauses as subjects and objects.
Form simple and complex indirect questions with statement word order.
overview.outcome: By the end you can make a full complaint and request a solution using at least three indirect questions.

vocab.term: to have a bone to pick with
vocab.def: to have a reason to complain to someone.
vocab.use: Semi-humorous and personal — used with people you know, not with a shop assistant.
examples: I’ve got a bone to pick with you about last night.
She had a bone to pick with her landlord.
vocab.colloc: have a bone to pick with someone

vocab.def: not working correctly; defective.
vocab.use: Standard word for consumer complaints. For a service, use ‘poor’; for reasoning, ‘flawed’.
examples: The charger was faulty from the first day.
We’re recalling faulty units free of charge.
vocab.colloc: a faulty product · faulty wiring · return a faulty item

vocab.def: money returned to you when you take a product back.
vocab.use: As a noun with ‘get / give / ask for’; as a verb, ‘they refunded the money’. Compare ‘exchange’.
examples: I’d like a full refund rather than a replacement.
They refunded me within three days.
vocab.colloc: a full refund · ask for a refund · a no-refund policy

vocab.def: to tolerate something unpleasant without complaining.
vocab.use: Three parts, never separable: put up with it. The formal equivalent is ‘tolerate’.
examples: I’m not putting up with that noise another night.
She put up with the situation for years.
vocab.colloc: put up with noise · have to put up with · refuse to put up with

vocab.def: to complain or worry more than a situation deserves.
vocab.use: Often used to describe someone else’s reaction, or to excuse your own: ‘I don’t want to make a fuss, but…’
examples: I don’t want to make a fuss, but this isn’t what I ordered.
He made a huge fuss about a five-minute delay.
vocab.colloc: make a fuss about something · without making a fuss

vocab.def: the final small problem that makes a situation unbearable.
vocab.use: Refers to something minor in itself — that is the point of the idiom.
examples: The cancelled flight was the last straw.
When they lost my order again, that was the last straw.
vocab.colloc: the last straw · the final straw

vocab.def: to pass a complaint to a higher level, or to become more serious.
vocab.use: Transitive and intransitive: “escalate the complaint”, “the dispute escalated”.
examples: I had to escalate it to the manager.
The argument escalated quickly.
vocab.colloc: escalate a complaint · escalate quickly

vocab.def: something a company gives to keep a customer happy.
vocab.use: “As a goodwill gesture, they refunded the delivery.” Countable.
examples: They offered a voucher as a goodwill gesture.
It was a goodwill gesture, not compensation.
vocab.colloc: as a goodwill gesture · a small goodwill gesture

vocab.def: to refuse to give in under pressure.
vocab.use: No object: “I stood my ground and got the refund.”
examples: She stood her ground and they replaced the item.
Stand your ground — you’re entitled to a refund.
vocab.colloc: stand your ground · hold your ground

vocab.def: formal compensation for something that went wrong.
vocab.use: Uncountable and formal: “seek redress”, “a means of redress”.
examples: Customers have little redress in these cases.
They sought redress through the courts.
vocab.colloc: seek redress · legal redress

vocab.term: to take something up with someone
vocab.def: to raise a complaint with the person who can act on it.
vocab.use: Three parts, fixed order: “take it up with the manager”.
examples: I’d take it up with the supplier rather than the shop.
She took the charge up with her bank and got it reversed.
vocab.colloc: take it up with someone · take the matter up

vocab.term: to be at the end of your tether
vocab.def: to have no patience left.
vocab.use: British; the American version is “at the end of my rope”. Used to justify a complaint.
examples: After the fourth delivery failed I was at the end of my tether.
He sounded polite, but he was clearly at the end of his tether.
vocab.colloc: at the end of my tether · reach the end of your tether

grammar.name: Noun clauses and relative clauses
grammar.short: What annoys me is… / the item that broke.
grammar.rule: A noun clause does the job of a noun — subject or object of the sentence. A relative clause does the job of an adjective, describing a noun that is already there.
form: Noun clause as subject: What annoys me is the noise.
Noun clause as object: I don’t understand why they charged me twice.
Relative clause: The product that I bought is faulty.
notes: Noun clauses keep statement word order even when they start with a question word.
‘What’ in a noun clause means ‘the thing that’ — don’t add ‘that’ as well.
A noun-clause subject takes a singular verb: ‘What worries me is the delays.’
examples: What annoys me most is the constant noise.
The product that I bought last week is already faulty.
I don’t understand why they charged me twice.
grammar.watch: Don’t write ‘What that annoys me…’ — ‘what’ already contains ‘the thing that’.
grammar.deep: Noun clauses and relative clauses look alike and do opposite things. A noun clause fills a slot in the sentence — subject, object or complement — and can be replaced by “something”: “I don’t know what he wants” (I don’t know something). A relative clause modifies a noun already present and can be deleted without breaking the structure: “the thing that he wants” (the thing is still there). Mixing them produces the two commonest errors at this level: inverting a noun clause as if it were a question (“I don’t know what does he want”) and leaving a relative clause with no noun to attach to. A useful test is substitution. If “something” or “the fact” fits, you have a noun clause; if the clause is answering “which one?”, you have a relative clause.
more: What annoys me most is being told the delay is normal.
The part that irritates me is the automated apology.
What I don’t understand is why nobody answers the phone.
The person who took my order never wrote it down.
What I’d like is a refund, not an explanation.
The one thing that would fix this is a named contact.

fix.wrong: What annoys me are the delays.
fix.right: What annoys me is the delays.
fix.why: A what-clause subject takes a singular verb.

fix.wrong: The thing what bothers me is the noise.
fix.right: The thing that bothers me is the noise.
fix.why: “What” cannot follow a noun; use “that”.

fix.wrong: What I want is to you refund the charge.
fix.right: What I want is for you to refund the charge.
fix.why: An infinitive with its own subject needs “for”.

drill.name: Front the complaint
drill.prompt: Turn each complaint into a what-clause, then again with “the thing that…”.

dialogue.line: So what’s the actual problem?
What annoys me is that nobody told us.
The delay itself is fine?
The delay I can live with. The thing that bothers me is the silence.

contrast.title: Which frame for a complaint
rows: What annoys me is the wait.
The thing that broke is the handle.
What I’d like is a refund.
The reason I’m calling is that…
What annoys me is the delays.

grammar.sound: The fronted clause ends on a rise and the stress lands after “is”: “what ANNOYS me is ↑ the SILence”. That rise is what buys you the listener’s attention before the complaint arrives.

grammar.name: Indirect questions
grammar.short: Could you tell me where the manager is?
grammar.rule: An indirect question wraps a question inside a polite introductory phrase. The inner question loses its inversion and its auxiliary ‘do’.
form: Introductory phrase + question word + subject + verb: Could you tell me where the fitting rooms are?
With no question word, use if / whether: Do you know if this is refundable?
Common openers: Could you tell me… · Do you know… · I was wondering… · Would you mind telling me…
notes: Delete ‘do / does / did’ completely: ‘I wonder what it costs’, not ‘what does it cost’.
If the sentence starts with ‘Could you…’ it takes a question mark; if it starts with ‘I was wondering…’ it takes a full stop.
‘Whether’ is slightly more formal than ‘if’ and is the only option before ‘or not’.
examples: Could you tell me when it will be fixed?
Do you know if this is refundable?
I was wondering whether you could help me with a return.
grammar.watch: Statement word order inside: ‘where the manager is’, never ‘where is the manager’.
grammar.deep: An indirect question embeds the question inside a larger frame, and the embedded clause reverts to statement order with no auxiliary “do”. That is the mechanical rule, and it applies whether the frame is a question (“Could you tell me…?”) or a statement (“I’d like to know…”). What matters at B2 is the pragmatics. Indirect questions buy politeness and distance, which is why they dominate service encounters, formal emails and any situation where a direct question would sound like an interrogation. They also let you stack softeners: “I was wondering whether you might be able to…” is four layers of hedging on one request. The punctuation follows the frame, not the content: a question frame takes a question mark, a statement frame takes a full stop, and yes/no questions inside take “if” or “whether”.

chart.title: Direct to indirect
rows: Could you tell me where the manager is?
Do you know when it closes?
I wonder whether you sent it.
I’d like to know how much it is.
Could you tell me if I can get a refund?

more: Could you tell me where the complaints department is?
I was wondering whether you could check the order number.
Do you happen to know when the manager gets back?
Would you mind telling me why the charge appeared twice?
I’d like to know who authorised the change.
Could you explain what happens if the part doesn’t arrive?

fix.wrong: Could you tell me where is the manager?
fix.right: Could you tell me where the manager is?
fix.why: An indirect question keeps statement word order.

fix.wrong: I was wondering can you check it.
fix.right: I was wondering whether you could check it.
fix.why: The embedded clause needs “if” or “whether” and a past-form modal.

fix.wrong: Do you know when does it open?
fix.right: Do you know when it opens?
fix.why: No auxiliary “does” appears in the embedded clause.

drill.name: Make it indirect
drill.prompt: Turn each blunt question into an indirect one, using a different opener each time.

dialogue.line: Could you tell me why the charge is still showing?
It can take five days.
I was wondering whether you could confirm that in writing.
Of course. Do you happen to know the reference number?

grammar.sound: The whole indirect question is spoken on a gentle fall, not the rise of a direct question. A rising tone at the end makes the politeness sound sarcastic.

speaking.text: A customer returns a faulty product to a shop assistant – complain politely and reach a solution.
This house believes people complain far too much these days. Agree or disagree.
Turn three blunt complaints into polite, indirect ones with your partner.

tips: Indirect questions use statement word order: ‘Could you tell me where it is?’ (not ‘where is it’).
Use ‘if’ or ‘whether’ when there’s no question word: ‘Do you know if it’s open?’
Common slip: drop ‘do / does / did’ in an indirect question – ‘I wonder what it costs’, not ‘what does it cost’.

quiz.explain: Indirect questions use statement word order: ‘where the fitting rooms are’.

dynamics.name: Complaints desk
dynamics.how: Half the class staff a desk, half bring a written complaint. Complainants must open with a what-clause and ask two indirect questions; staff may only resolve it if both appear. Rotate twice.
dynamics.payoff: The rule of entry makes the structures obligatory rather than optional.

dynamics.name: Blunt to diplomatic
dynamics.how: Groups receive eight blunt demands and rewrite each as an indirect question, then perform the pair aloud. The class marks any that became so polite the request disappeared.
dynamics.payoff: Teaches that over-hedging has a cost, which stops mechanical politeness.

dynamics.name: Escalation ladder
dynamics.how: Groups take one complaint through four stages — counter staff, supervisor, written complaint, public review — changing register at each step while keeping the same facts.
dynamics.payoff: Shows the same content across four registers, which is what B2 needs.

dynamics.name: What annoys me most
dynamics.how: Every student says one what-clause complaint about daily life; the class groups them on the board and votes on the most universal. Any wrong verb agreement is corrected by the group.
dynamics.payoff: Fast, high-volume production of the target frame.

writing.title: A letter of complaint
writing.brief: Write a formal complaint about a real product or service. Open with a what-clause that states your reaction, give the facts in order, ask two indirect questions, and close with the outcome you want.
criteria: Three noun-clause or cleft frames, all with singular agreement.
Two indirect questions with statement word order.
One sentence stating the remedy you expect, with a deadline.

homework.title: Five frames, five questions
homework.task: Write five complaints about things that annoy you, each fronted with a what-clause or “the thing that…”. Then turn five blunt questions into indirect ones, using a different opener for each.

test.q: What annoys me ___ the automated replies.
test.explain: A what-clause subject is singular.

test.q: The thing ___ bothers me is the silence.
test.explain: “What” cannot follow a noun.

test.q: Could you tell me where ___ ?
test.explain: Indirect questions keep statement word order.

test.q: I was wondering ___ you could check the order.
test.explain: A yes/no question embeds with if or whether.

test.q: Would you mind ___ me why it was cancelled?
test.explain: “Would you mind” takes a gerund.

Under it, THE THING THAT … IS …, and a red box crossing out “the thing what”.
Centre: DIRECT vs INDIRECT written as two columns, one question shown in both forms with the inversion visibly undone by an arrow.
Lower left: openers — Could you tell me · Do you know · I was wondering whether · Would you mind + -ing.
Bottom strip: an intonation arrow falling at the end of the indirect question, with “rise = sarcasm” noted.

units.title: VALUES
units.theme: Ethics, hypothetical situations, wishes and regrets

overview.intro: Ethical discussion is hypothetical by nature: what would you do, what if nobody found out, what do you wish you had done? This unit builds the unreal conditional and the language of regret so you can argue about values, not just describe them.
goals: Discuss honesty, principles and dilemmas with precise vocabulary.
Use the present unreal conditional, including unless, only if and even if.
Express present wishes and past regrets accurately.
overview.outcome: By the end you can argue a moral dilemma using three unreal conditionals and express one regret with ‘if only’.

vocab.def: the quality of being honest and having strong moral principles.
vocab.use: Uncountable and always positive. Common in references and job descriptions.
examples: She’s a leader of real integrity.
The scandal damaged the company’s integrity.
vocab.colloc: personal / professional integrity · a person of integrity

vocab.def: to defend a person or a belief.
vocab.use: Three parts, inseparable. ‘Stand up to’ is different — it means resist someone powerful.
examples: He stood up for a colleague nobody else would defend.
Stand up for what you believe, even alone.
vocab.colloc: stand up for yourself · stand up for your beliefs

vocab.def: a difficult choice between two options, often both unattractive.
vocab.use: Strictly two options — that is what ‘di-’ means. Use ‘difficult decision’ for more.
examples: She faced a real dilemma: tell the truth or protect her friend.
It’s an ethical dilemma with no easy answer.
vocab.colloc: face a dilemma · an ethical / moral dilemma

vocab.def: to begin to doubt a decision you have made.
vocab.use: Takes ‘about’: second thoughts about the job. Implies the decision was already taken.
examples: I’m having second thoughts about accepting the offer.
He signed, then had second thoughts overnight.
vocab.colloc: have second thoughts about something · serious second thoughts

vocab.def: acting on firm moral rules.
vocab.use: A compliment; ‘unprincipled’ is a strong insult. Compare ‘stubborn’, which is negative.
examples: It was a principled decision that cost him the job.
She’s too principled to accept the gift.
vocab.colloc: a principled stand · highly principled

vocab.def: to set a limit on what you will accept or do.
vocab.use: Takes ‘at’ for the limit: ‘I draw the line at lying.’
examples: I’ll bend the rules, but I draw the line at lying.
Everyone has to draw the line somewhere.
vocab.colloc: draw the line at something · draw a clear line

vocab.def: to feel uneasy about whether something is right.
vocab.use: Usually negative or plural: “I have no qualms about reporting it.”
examples: She had qualms about accepting the money.
I have no qualms about saying no.
vocab.colloc: have no qualms about · serious qualms

vocab.def: an internal sense of right and wrong.
vocab.use: Countable, usually singular with a possessive: “his moral compass”.
examples: He seems to have lost his moral compass.
A strong moral compass matters more than rules.
vocab.colloc: a strong moral compass · lose your moral compass

vocab.def: to settle by each side giving up something; or to damage a principle.
vocab.use: Two senses: “reach a compromise” (positive) and “compromise your values” (negative).
examples: We reached a compromise after an hour.
He refused to compromise his principles.
vocab.colloc: reach a compromise · compromise your integrity

vocab.def: moral hesitations about doing something.
vocab.use: Almost always plural: “She has no scruples.” Adjective: unscrupulous.
examples: He has no scruples about undercutting rivals.
Her scruples cost her the contract.
vocab.colloc: have no scruples · moral scruples

vocab.def: a choice between two options that are both defensible or both wrong.
vocab.use: Formal but common in discussion: “it poses a moral dilemma”. Not a synonym for “problem”.
examples: Reporting a friend puts you in a genuine moral dilemma.
The case is a textbook moral dilemma.
vocab.colloc: face a moral dilemma · pose a dilemma · an ethical dilemma

grammar.name: Present unreal conditional
grammar.short: If + past, would + verb — plus unless, only if, even if.
grammar.rule: To imagine a present or future situation that is not real, use a past form in the if-clause and ‘would’ in the result clause. The past tense signals distance from reality, not past time.
form: If + past simple, would + base verb: If I had more time, I’d volunteer.
unless = if… not: I wouldn’t lie unless I had to.
only if = on this single condition · even if = whether or not: Even if they offered me a fortune, I’d refuse.
notes: ‘Were’ is used for all persons in careful English: ‘If I were you…’.
‘Could’ and ‘might’ can replace ‘would’ to weaken the result: ‘I might tell him.’
When ‘only if’ starts the sentence, the main clause inverts: ‘Only if he apologised would I forgive him.’
examples: If I were you, I’d tell the truth straight away.
I wouldn’t lie unless I absolutely had to.
Even if nobody ever found out, I’d still feel guilty.
grammar.watch: Keep ‘would’ out of the if-clause: ‘If I had time…’, not ‘If I would have time…’
grammar.deep: The present unreal conditional is the grammar of argument and imagination: an if-clause in the past simple and a result clause with would, could or might. The past form is not past time — it is a marker of unreality, the same backshift you use after “wish”. Three refinements matter at B2. “Were” is the standard form for all persons in careful English (“if I were in her position”), and “if I were you” remains the most natural way to give strong advice. The result clause can swap “would” for “could” (ability), “might” (uncertain outcome) or “would have to” (consequence), each changing the claim. And the more formal inversion “were I to accept…” drops “if” entirely, which is worth recognising in reading even if you rarely produce it.

chart.title: Present unreal conditional
rows: I could help if I finished early.
She might agree if you asked.
If I were you, I’d wait.
Were we to accept, we’d need approval.

more: If I found a wallet with two thousand euros in it, I’d hand it in — probably.
If she weren’t his sister, nobody would defend the decision.
Unless the money were traceable, most people would keep it.
I’d say something only if I were certain.
Even if they apologised, I wouldn’t work with them again.
If it were my company, I’d publish the whole report.

fix.wrong: If I would have more time, I’d volunteer.
fix.right: If I had more time, I’d volunteer.
fix.why: “Would” belongs in the result clause, never in the if-clause.

fix.wrong: If I was you, I’d refuse.
fix.right: If I were you, I’d refuse.
fix.why: In the fixed advice formula, the subjunctive “were” is the standard form.

fix.wrong: Unless you don’t tell him, he’ll never know.
fix.right: Unless you tell him, he’ll never know.
fix.why: “Unless” already means “if not”.

drill.name: Would you, though
drill.prompt: Answer each dilemma with a full conditional, then add a condition that would change your answer.
items: you find a wallet in the street
a friend asks you to lie for them
you’re offered a job you’re unqualified for

dialogue.line: If you found the money, would you keep it?
If there were no name on the wallet, maybe.
And if there were?
Then I’d hand it in. I’d only keep it if there were genuinely no way to return it.

contrast.title: Second conditional and its neighbours
rows: If I had time, I’d go.
I’d agree only if it were public.
If I asked, she might agree.

grammar.sound: “Would” contracts onto the subject — “I’d”, “they’d” — so the only audible sign of the conditional is often a single /d/. Hitting the past-tense verb in the if-clause is what keeps the sentence intelligible.

grammar.name: Wishes and regrets
grammar.short: wish + past / past perfect / would.
grammar.rule: ‘Wish’ and ‘if only’ shift one tense back from the reality you are describing. The tense you choose shows whether you regret the present, the past, or someone else’s behaviour.
form: Present wish: wish + past simple — I wish I had more free time.
Past regret: wish + past perfect — If only I had said sorry.
Annoyance at others: wish + would — I wish people wouldn’t drop litter.
notes: ‘If only’ is simply a more emphatic ‘I wish’.
You cannot use ‘wish + would’ about yourself — use ‘wish I could’ instead.
‘I wish I were…’ is preferred to ‘I wish I was…’ in formal English.
examples: I wish I had more free time during the week.
If only I had said sorry when I had the chance.
I wish people wouldn’t leave their rubbish behind.
grammar.watch: ‘Wish + past simple’ = present wish; ‘wish + past perfect’ = past regret. Mixing them changes the meaning entirely.
grammar.deep: Wishes and regrets run on the same unreality backshift, one step further back for the past. A present wish takes the past simple (“I wish I spoke Mandarin”), a past regret takes the past perfect (“I wish I had spoken up”), and an annoyance about someone else’s behaviour takes “would” (“I wish you would listen”). The last of these is a complaint rather than a wish, and it is only possible about other people, not about yourself. Alongside them sits “if only”, which is emphatic and can stand alone as a full utterance. Two lines to keep clean: “hope” is for possible futures and “wish” for the contrary-to-fact, and “should have” is the modal alternative for regrets about your own decisions — “I wish I hadn’t agreed” and “I shouldn’t have agreed” differ in emotion, not in fact.

chart.title: Wishes and regrets
rows: I wish I could tell you.
I wish I had said no.

more: I wish I had said something at the time.
I wish I spoke better Portuguese — it would have changed that whole year.
She wishes she hadn’t sent the message at two in the morning.
I wish they would stop asking me about it.
If only we had left an hour earlier.
I wish I were the kind of person who could let it go.

fix.wrong: I wish I would have said something.
fix.right: I wish I had said something.
fix.why: A regret about the past takes “wish + past perfect”.

fix.wrong: I wish he stops interrupting.
fix.right: I wish he would stop interrupting.
fix.why: A wish about someone else’s behaviour takes “would”.

fix.wrong: I wish I can speak Italian.
fix.right: I wish I could speak Italian.
fix.why: “Wish” requires the past form of the modal.

drill.name: Present or past regret
drill.prompt: For each item, make a wish about now and a wish about the past.

dialogue.line: Do you regret taking it?
I wish I’d asked more questions first.
Would you leave now?
I wish it were that simple. And I wish they’d tell us what’s actually happening.

contrast.title: wish, and what follows it
rows: I wish I had more time.

grammar.sound: “I wish I’d” compresses to /aɪ wɪʃ aɪd/, and the whole time reference rests on that final /d/. Learners who drop it turn a past regret into a present one.

speaking.text: Two friends find a lost wallet full of cash and argue over the right thing to do.
This house believes honesty is always the best policy. Argue for or against.
Share a decision you have second thoughts about, using ‘I wish…’ and ‘If only…’.

tips: In the second conditional, use ‘were’ for all subjects: ‘If I were rich…’.
‘wish + past simple’ = a present wish; ‘wish + past perfect’ = a past regret.
Common slip: ‘unless’ already means ‘if… not’ – don’t add another ‘not’.

quiz.q: I ___ take the money even if no one was watching.
quiz.explain: The present unreal conditional uses ‘would(n’t) + base verb’: ‘wouldn’t take’.

dynamics.name: Dilemma cards
dynamics.how: Each group takes four ethical dilemmas and must reach a group answer for each, with every contribution framed as a conditional. Any bare answer is ruled out of order by the group’s referee.
dynamics.payoff: The referee role keeps the structure obligatory without the teacher policing it.

dynamics.name: Regret market
dynamics.how: Students write three regrets on slips and trade them for the regret they find most interesting, then explain to the class why they chose it, using “they wish they had…”.
dynamics.payoff: Reporting other people’s wishes forces the third person, which is where the tense slips.

dynamics.name: If I were you
dynamics.how: A brings a real minor problem; B advises with three sentences, one “If I were you…”, one “I’d only … if…”, one “Even if…”. Then swap.
dynamics.payoff: Three different conditional shapes in one short exchange.

dynamics.name: Value ranking
dynamics.how: Groups rank six values (honesty, loyalty, fairness…) and must defend each placement with a hypothetical situation in the second conditional. Other groups may attack with “What if…?”
dynamics.payoff: Abstract values become concrete only through hypotheticals.

writing.title: A decision I would take differently
writing.brief: Describe a decision you made that you now question. Explain what you would do if you faced it today, what you wish you had done then, and what would have to be true for you to change your mind again.
criteria: Four second conditionals, one with unless, only if or even if.
Three wishes covering the present, the past and someone else’s behaviour.
No “would” inside an if-clause.

homework.title: Six hypotheticals, six wishes
homework.task: Answer six ethical dilemmas in full second conditionals, adding one condition that would change your answer. Then write six wishes: two about now, two about the past, two about other people’s behaviour.

test.q: If I ___ more time, I’d volunteer.
test.explain: The if-clause takes the past simple, never “would”.

test.q: If I ___ you, I’d refuse.
test.explain: The advice formula uses “were”.

test.q: ___ you ask, nobody will offer.
test.explain: “Unless” means “if not” and needs no second negative.

test.q: I wish I ___ something at the time.
test.explain: A past regret takes “wish + past perfect”.

test.q: I wish he ___ interrupting.
test.explain: A wish about someone else’s behaviour takes “would”.

board: Top: IF + PAST SIMPLE , WOULD + VERB written large, with a red arrow showing WOULD only on the right of the comma.
Beside it, a crossed-out “If I would have time”.
Centre: the three neighbours — UNLESS · ONLY IF · EVEN IF — each with one example.
Lower half: WISH + past simple (now) / + past perfect (then) / + would (other people), as three stacked rows.
Bottom strip: IF ONLY … , with two examples the class supplies.

units.title: MOVING AROUND
units.theme: Travel, culture shock and future life plans

overview.intro: The final unit looks forwards and backwards at once: what you will have achieved by a future date, and how a different past would have produced a different present. Mixed conditionals are the most advanced structure in the course — and the most satisfying to control.
goals: Talk about relocating, culture shock and adaptation with natural vocabulary.
Use the future perfect and future perfect continuous with time markers.
Combine time frames in mixed conditional sentences.
overview.outcome: By the end you can describe your life five years from now with two future perfect sentences, and explain one turning point using a mixed conditional.

vocab.def: the disorientation felt in an unfamiliar culture.
vocab.use: Usually uncountable: ‘I experienced culture shock.’ Also ‘reverse culture shock’ on returning home.
examples: The first month abroad was pure culture shock.
Nobody warns you about reverse culture shock.
vocab.colloc: experience culture shock · suffer from culture shock

vocab.def: to become comfortable in a new place or situation.
vocab.use: Intransitive; takes time expressions: settle in quickly, take a while to settle in.
examples: It took me six months to settle in properly.
They’ve settled in well at the new school.
vocab.colloc: settle in quickly · take time to settle in

vocab.def: sad because you miss your home and family.
vocab.use: Predicative: ‘I felt homesick’. The noun is ‘homesickness’.
examples: I got terribly homesick during the first winter.
She was homesick for her mother’s cooking.
vocab.colloc: feel / get homesick · homesick for somewhere

vocab.def: to gain wider knowledge and experience.
vocab.use: Positive and slightly formal — common in motivation letters and interviews.
examples: Living abroad broadened my horizons more than any course.
Reading widely broadens your horizons.
vocab.colloc: broaden your horizons · widen your horizons

vocab.def: a person living outside their native country.
vocab.use: ‘Expat’ is the everyday short form. The word carries assumptions of choice, unlike ‘immigrant’ — worth discussing.
examples: There’s a large expat community in the city.
He’s been an expat for over a decade.
vocab.colloc: an expat community · the expat life

vocab.def: to travel from place to place within an area.
vocab.use: Also means ‘avoid’ a rule (‘get around the regulations’) — context makes it clear.
examples: It’s easy to get around by metro.
Without a car, getting around is a challenge.
vocab.colloc: get around by bus · easy to get around · get around the city

vocab.def: to settle permanently in a place.

grammar.name: Future perfect and future perfect continuous
grammar.short: By 2030 I’ll have finished / I’ll have been living here for ten years.
grammar.rule: The future perfect looks back from a point in the future: it describes an action completed before that point. The continuous form describes an activity still in progress up to it, stressing duration.
form: will have + past participle: By next year, I’ll have visited five countries.
will have been + -ing: By June, we’ll have been travelling for six months.
Time markers: by then, by 2030, by the time…, in two years.
notes: A future time marker is essentially obligatory — without one the tense makes no sense.
After ‘by the time’, use the present tense, not ‘will’: ‘by the time you arrive’.
Use the continuous only with action verbs; ‘will have known’ stays simple.
examples: By next year, I’ll have visited five new countries.
By June, we’ll have been travelling for six months.
They’ll have settled in by the time you arrive.
grammar.watch: ‘By the time you WILL arrive’ is wrong — time clauses stay in the present.
grammar.deep: The future perfect and future perfect continuous look forwards from a point that has not arrived yet and report backwards from it. “By December I will have finished the course” places a completion before a future deadline; “By December I will have been studying for two years” measures the duration up to that deadline. Both need a future reference point, which is why “by”, “by the time” and “in three years” are almost obligatory. Two mechanics: after “by the time” the verb stays in the present (“by the time you arrive”), following the same rule as all time clauses; and the continuous version follows the usual restriction on state verbs, so “I will have known her for ten years” cannot become continuous. These tenses are the natural language of plans, targets and projections.

drill.name: By then

dialogue.line: When does the visa expire?
In April. By then I’ll have been here three years.
And the application?

grammar.name: Mixed conditionals
grammar.short: Past cause → present result, or present cause → past result.
grammar.rule: A mixed conditional combines two different time frames in one sentence, because a past event can have a present consequence, and a permanent present fact can explain a past outcome.
form: Past → present: If I had saved more, I’d be travelling now.
Present → past: If I weren’t so shy, I’d have spoken up.
Structure: If + past perfect, would + base · If + past simple, would have + p.p.
notes: Look for a present time word (now, today, still) in the result to spot type one.
The if-clause with a present meaning usually describes a permanent characteristic.
Both halves remain hypothetical — neither actually happened.
examples: If I had saved more last year, I’d be travelling right now.
If she were more organised, she wouldn’t have missed the flight.
If we’d left earlier, we’d be there by now.
grammar.watch: Decide the time of each half separately — that decision alone tells you which forms to use.
grammar.deep: A mixed conditional puts the condition in one time frame and the result in another, which is exactly what real regret usually requires. The commonest pattern runs from a past condition to a present result: “If I had taken that job, I would be living in Lima now” — the decision is past, the consequence is current. The reverse also exists: a present condition with a past result, “If I weren’t so cautious, I would have accepted”, where a permanent characteristic explains a past choice. Building them is a matter of choosing each half independently: past unreal condition uses the past perfect, present unreal condition uses the past simple; a past result uses “would have + participle”, a present result uses “would + base verb”. Recognising which half belongs to which time is what makes the sentence say what you mean.

now / today / then / at the time

If he spoke the language, he wouldn’t have missed the announcement.

fix.wrong: If I had taken that job, I would have lived in Lima now.
fix.right: If I had taken that job, I would be living in Lima now.
fix.why: A present result takes “would + base verb”, not “would have”.

fix.wrong: If I wouldn’t be so cautious, I would have accepted.
fix.right: If I weren’t so cautious, I would have accepted.
fix.why: The if-clause never takes “would”.

fix.wrong: If she had stayed, she can help us today.
fix.right: If she had stayed, she could help us today.
fix.why: An unreal present result requires the past-form modal.

a person you lost touch with

dialogue.line: Do you regret turning down Santiago?
If I’d taken it, I’d be fluent by now.
So why didn’t you?
If I weren’t so attached to my routine, I would have gone without thinking.

contrast.title: Mixed conditionals
rows: If I’d studied, I’d be a doctor now.
If she’d stayed, she could help today.
If I weren’t shy, I would have spoken.
If I had time, I’d go.
If I’d known, I’d have called.

grammar.sound: The two halves are told apart entirely by what follows “would”: /wʊd bi/ for a present result, /wʊdəv/ for a past one. That one syllable carries the whole time reference.

speaking.text: An expat advises someone about to move abroad – cover culture shock and settling in.
This house believes living abroad is the best way to broaden your horizons. Argue for or against.
Describe where you’ll have travelled and what you’ll have achieved five years from now.

tips: The future perfect needs a future time marker: ‘by 2027’, ‘by the time…’, ‘in two years’.
Mixed conditionals join a past ‘if’-clause with a present result, or the reverse.
Common slip: after ‘by the time’ use the present, not the future: ‘by the time you arrive’, not ‘will arrive’.

quiz.q: By this time next year, I ___ my degree.
quiz.explain: The future perfect (‘will have + past participle’) describes an action completed by a future point.

dynamics.name: Ten years from Friday
dynamics.how: Each student writes six predictions about a partner’s life at a named future date, all in the future perfect. The partner accepts, rejects or amends each one aloud with a duration.
dynamics.payoff: Predictions about a real person get argued about, which produces the continuous form too.

dynamics.name: Parallel lives
dynamics.how: Each student names a decision they nearly took; the group builds the alternative present in mixed conditionals — where they would be living, what they would be doing. Every sentence must mix time frames.
dynamics.payoff: Mixed conditionals are exactly the grammar of the road not taken.

dynamics.name: Visa queue
dynamics.how: Groups receive four relocation cases with dates and must state, for each, what will have happened and how long each person will have been waiting by a given deadline. Groups then swap and check the arithmetic and the tense.
dynamics.payoff: Dates make the deadline structure obligatory and checkable.

dynamics.name: Would be or would have
dynamics.how: The teacher reads half a conditional; students complete it and must say whether the result is present or past. Any mismatch passes the turn.
dynamics.payoff: Drills the single syllable that distinguishes the two results.

writing.title: Where I’ll be and where I nearly was
writing.brief: Write two paragraphs. In the first, describe your life at a named future date using future perfect forms. In the second, describe the life you would be living now if one past decision had gone the other way.
criteria: Three future perfect sentences, one continuous with a duration.
Three mixed conditionals, at least one running present cause to past result.
No “would” in any if-clause.

homework.title: Six deadlines, six alternative lives
homework.task: Write six future-perfect sentences with real dates, marking which are simple and which continuous and why. Then write six mixed conditionals about decisions you nearly took, three from past cause to present result and three the other way.
